PERFORMING — Anchor Standard 4: Select, Analyze, and Interpret Artistic Work for Presentation

Enduring Understanding: Space, time, and energy are basic elements of dance.

Essential Question: How do dancers work with space, time, and energy to communicate artistic expression?

Process Component: Express

PK.DA:Pr4

a. Identify and demonstrate directions for moving the body in general space (e.g., forward, backwards, sideways, up, down, and turning) and finding and returning to a place in space.

b. Identify speed of movement as fast or slow. Move to varied rhythmic sounds at different tempi.

c. Move with opposing dynamics.

Circle-Up

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. OK, show me your thumb scale!” Briefly acknowledge each student’s level with a neutral, appreciative response.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students, “In our final classes together we are going rehearse our three dances for our end-of-year performance! One of the main roles (or jobs) of a performer is to be confident in their performance, and that takes a lot of practice!”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Have you ever tried to do something and at first you didn’t succeed? Maybe you tried to swing a bat, or maybe you tried to do a cartwheel, or maybe you tried to play a song on the piano. Performers, whether they are a gymnast, a basketball player, or a dancer, all do one thing, they practice until they get good at it.

The Role of the Performer
Explain to students that after all these weeks of practice and rehearsal, it is now time to get ready for the performance. Tell students:

“Let’s warm up our bodies so that we can review and rehearse our dances, and prepare for the performance.”

Hello/Goodbye Toes

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello, toes!” followed by pointing the feet and saying, “Goodbye, toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Finish by bending the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet. Lift the head up, trying to lengthen the spine and flex the feet saying, “Hello, toes!” and then round the spine forward, nodding the head down and pointing the feet (keeping hands resting on the top of the foot/ankle) and say, “Goodbye, toes.” Repeat 3-5 times.

Butterfly Trip

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be a real or pretend location). Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and “put on their brakes,” making a soft squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Make a Pizza

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to make a pretend pizza! Begin by asking, “What is the first thing we need to make a pizza?” Take 2-3 suggestions from students. Then say, “We need pizza dough!” Model and tell students to follow: shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (sauce, cheese, etc.). You can ask students for individual toppings and place them all around the imaginary pizza, getting a forward stretch each time. Remind students to try and keep their legs straight, “ so their pizza stays flat and doesn’t get squished.”

Now it is time for the pizza to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pizza inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pizza to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pizza knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pizza is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pizza out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch, eat the other side, and then eat all the pizza in the middle), keeping legs as straight as possible.

Countdown

Bring all students to a standing position in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1.

Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Intro

“We have learned so many ways to move our bodies and dance this year! Let’s practice some of the activities we’ve learned.

Obstacle Course (Procedure)

To set up this activity, create one-to-two parallel courses in the open floor space so that students can quickly move through each station of the course. Designate the starting line and the finish line with a cone or poly dot. Review each element individually, then combine into an obstacle course where each element is linked to the next.

Relevé Walks

Place a “ladder” of 8 artificial rose stems on the floor. Instruct students to rise onto their tip toes and step ‘en relevé’ over each rose, careful not to touch the thorny stems. Body stays tall and lifted. *Can add a passé/high knee for a more advanced variation.

Heel/Toe Backward Walk: Take slow, careful steps backwards, touching toe to heel for each step from point A to point B (marked by cones or poly dots), hands on hips or out to side for balance.

Airplane Walk

Place 6 cones in a line and instruct students to zigzag around each cone with arms out to the side like an airplane.

Hoop Hops:

Place 5 hula hoops on the floor in a row and have students jump into each one with both feet, hands on hips, careful not to touch the hoops or lose their balance.

Over the River

Place a large blue scarf or towel on the floor, and explain to the students that the scarf represents a river of water, and they are going to jump over the “river.” Instruct them not to step in the river (touch the scarf), and try to help them leap with one foot extending out in front and landing on the same front foot (like a grande jeté).

Intro

“Now let’s practice all three of our dances so we can really show off what we have learned and perform with confidence!”

Review Choreography for Dance #1, #2, and #3

Arrange students in window formation. Review the choreography for all dances, practice and repeat movements as necessary. Remember to switch lines periodically to ensure all students can see the teacher from the front row.

Entrance/Exit

“Next I’m going to teach you how to enter and exit the stage for a performance.” Once students have reviewed all dances, teach them the procedure (and purpose) for their entrance and exit. Begin by reminding students of the designated audience and performance spaces in the classroom.* Explain that a performer begins from the moment they enter the stage. This means that as they enter, they must walk with stage presence. Tell students, “We practice stage presence every time we are in Dancer Position. This means standing tall with confidence, having control of our bodies, and keeping our voices silent.”

Begin with the students “off stage,” and teach them how to quietly and quickly walk to their designated space on stage for the first dance. If it is helpful, you may use poly dots to mark the students’ positions in windows (or any other spacing required for the choreography). After students have learned and practiced how to enter the stage area, rehearse a final group bow, and how to exit the stage in an organized, quiet line.

*If you will be performing in another location and have access to the stage at this time, it is recommended that you rehearse in the final location, if possible.

",,"

Arrange students seated in a circle and ask, “What have been some of your favorite things about dance class? Tell us why you now feel more confident in dancing.” (practice) Invite 5-8 students to respond. Encourage the rest of the students to “silent shake” in agreement if they liked similar things being shared.

","

Bows

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer Position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

To finish, ask students to form a seated circle on the floor, the same way you began class. Instruct them to sit quietly and place one hand on top of their head. When you see that they are ready, place a sticker on the hand that is resting on their head.

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today you will get to create your own dance using different colors.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What are some colors that are NOT in the rainbow? Can you spot any in this room?” Invite 4-6 students to respond.

",,"
Favorite Color

“In the last class you shared one of your favorite colors. See if you can remember the color you chose and silently create a dance move that represents that color. For example, if your color was pink, your movement might show picking and smelling a pink flower.” Go around the circle and ask students to share their color name and the corresponding movement. Continue until each student has had a turn.
“Doing this helped me get to know something more about each of you. Show me with a thumbs up if you enjoyed learning about each other as you all shared a movement with us.”

,

Point/Flex Toes (Color Variation)

“Audience Position!” Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Instruct students to flex and point their feet if they are wearing...red, blue, green, white, etc.

Finish by having all students bend the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet.

Butterfly Trip

Sit tall with legs in butterfly position, hands resting on top of the ankles. Tell students that we are going to fly somewhere that is blue. Ask students where we might fly to find blue (sky, ocean). Change colors as you go: Green (park), White (clouds), etc. Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and put on their brakes, making a quiet, squeaky brake sound.

Paint the Rainbow

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape, arms stretched out to each side. Explain that you are now going to paint all of the colors of the rainbow using our arms and hands as the paintbrush. Ask students, “What is the first color in the rainbow?” Then paint “red” by sweeping one arm up and over the body to meet the other arm, and lean over to one side. Holding that side stretch position, ask what the next color should be, and paint “orange” by reversing the direction of the arm sweep to arrive at the other side. Continue through all 6 colors of the rainbow: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple.

Color Countdown

Begin with students standing in Dancer Position. Explain that you will lift one arm overhead and shake it while saying the 6 colors of the rainbow, “Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple!” Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while repeating the 6 colors. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time saying the colors of the rainbow. Finally, shake your whole body and repeat the colors. All students should be saying the colors aloud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), saying one less color each time. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time, saying, “Red!” Finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

“Today you get to take turns being a performer and an audience. You will get to dance, and also watch each other dance. Please remember ‘Audience Position’ when you are part of the audience. You will be dancing with color again, this time showing how that color makes you feel!”

Color Scarf Free Dance

Sort small scarves into piles by color. Invite a small group of students to dance with a single color scarf that accompanies a music or rhythm that represents that color. For example, invite a group to dance with the yellow scarves and play a happy, upbeat song such as “Happy,” by Pharrel Williams. Next, invite a different group of students to use the red scarves and dance to a strong, bold piece of music such as “Symphony No. 5 by Ludwig Van Beethoven.”

Rotate groups so that there is enough room to freely dance, and remind students of “Audience Position” while they are not in the dancing group.

As students watch from the audience, ask them, “What movements did you notice? What stood out to you? How did dancing to a “color” make you feel?” Invite 2-3 students to respond after each group.

Dance #2 Choreography (Continued)

Begin by placing students in window formation. Review the first four 8-counts of choreography with students, practice and repeat movements as necessary. Remember to switch lines periodically to ensure all students can see the teacher from the front row. Continue to teach the next two to four 8-counts of choreography and add on to the previous steps.

*While choreography and song choice is at the discretion of the teacher, the movement should be reflective of the steps and dance elements students have learned in recent classes.

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

“Today we watched each other dance with different colored scarves to different ‘colors’ of music. Where else do we find colors when watching a dance performance?” Invite 3-5 students to respond and prompt them, if needed, with ideas such as costumes, lights, props, etc.

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

Paint the Rainbow

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape, arms stretched out to each side. Holding that side stretch position, ask what the next color should be, and paint “orange” by reversing the direction of the arm sweep to arrive at the other side. Begin with students standing in Dancer Position. Explain that you will lift one arm overhead and shake it while saying the 6 colors of the rainbow, “Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple!” Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while repeating the 6 colors. “Let’s warm up our bodies so that we can review and rehearse our dances, and prepare for the performance.”

Hello/Goodbye Toes

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello, toes!” followed by pointing the feet and saying, “Goodbye, toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Finish by bending the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet. Lift the head up, trying to lengthen the spine and flex the feet saying, “Hello, toes!” and then round the spine forward, nodding the head down and pointing the feet (keeping hands resting on the top of the foot/ankle) and say, “Goodbye, toes.” Repeat 3-5 times.

Butterfly Trip

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be a real or pretend location). Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and “put on their brakes,” making a soft squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Make a Pizza

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to make a pretend pizza! Begin by asking, “What is the first thing we need to make a pizza?” Take 2-3 suggestions from students. Then say, “We need pizza dough!” Model and tell students to follow: shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (sauce, cheese, etc.). You can ask students for individual toppings and place them all around the imaginary pizza, getting a forward stretch each time. Remind students to try and keep their legs straight, “ so their pizza stays flat and doesn’t get squished.”

Now it is time for the pizza to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pizza inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pizza to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pizza knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pizza is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pizza out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch, eat the other side, and then eat all the pizza in the middle), keeping legs as straight as possible.

Countdown

Bring all students to a standing position in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1.

Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Roller Coaster Breathing

Hold one hand open out in front of you, fingers stretched wide, use the other hand as a pointer finger and place your finger below the thumb knuckle on the opposite hand. As you trace your finger up the outside of your thumb, take a deep breath in and imagine you are on a rollercoaster, slowly making your way to the top. Then, trace your thumb down the other side, breathing out in a silent “scream” as you go down the rollercoaster. Repeat on each finger for 5 full breaths.

What is Stage Fright?

Ask students, “How many of you feel nervous about performing? This is known as stage fright and it is incredibly common, even for highly trained, professional performers! It can include physical symptoms such as an upset stomach, feeling like you have to use the bathroom frequently, or your hands feeling sweaty. The good news is that there are a number of things we can do as performers to feel less nervous.”

First, the more you perform, the easier it is to get in front of audiences, so keep performing when you have the opportunity!

Practice saying the following phrases before a performance:

  • I have prepared. I am ready. I’m gonna rock!
  • I know my dance backwards and forwards. I can do this with my eyes closed!

Take deep breaths (like our roller coaster breathing we did in warm up).

Talk about your nervous feelings with other performers and share! When you realize other people are also feeling nervous, it can remind you that you are not alone with these feelings.

“Think about the job YOU did as an audience today. Silent shake in agreement if you: watched the performers, listened, kept your voice off, kept your hands in your lap?”

Follow the Leader

Remind students that they get to lead the warm-up!

Review the procedure:

  1. Arrange students in window formation. Teacher stands at the front of the group.
  2. The teacher demonstrates a simple stretch or warm-up movement that students follow.
  3. The teacher will then walk behind a student and tap them gently on the shoulder.
  4. Once tapped, the student will move to the front of the room, and the teacher will stand in the student’s position in window formation.
  5. The student in front will lead the group in a new stretch or warm-up movement. Students follow.
  6. The teacher will then tap the shoulder of another student who will go to the front of the room, high-five the current student leader to switch spots, and lead the class in another new movement.
  7. The student in front returns to their original spot in the window formation.
  8. The teacher continues to tap on students to take turns leading the warm-up.

Review the Warm-Up Guidelines

Explain to students that there are a few ways to make their turn as leader successful. “The purpose of a warm-up is to safely prepare our body and mind for dance. This means that any move you do must be safe and possible for all dancers in the room (ie. don’t go into the splits, just because you can – that is not a move that everyone can do safely or at all!).” Next, remind them that in order to warm up the body evenly, any stretch or move that you do on one side of the body, you must also do on the other side. Lastly, “If you can’t think of a move to do, roll your wrists in a circle while you think of a move.”

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today’s class will be all about sports!

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Pretend I just arrived from another planet. Who can tell me what a ‘sport’ is?” Take student responses. “Do you think dance is a sport? Why or why not?” Discuss as a group, explaining that dance is both a sport and an art form. Both sports and dance are ways we use our bodies to show our strength, our talents, our emotions, and our imaginations!

*Share with students that in 2024, break dancing (a form of competitive hip-hop dance) was formally included as a sport in the Olympics!

",,"
Favorite Sport

Ask students, “What is one of your favorite sports to watch or play?” Popcorn response: point to each student and like popcorn popping up, allow each student to quickly go around the circle sharing their response. Then, arrange the students in groups based on their sport choice. For example, place all the students who chose basketball as their favorite sport in a group, football in a separate group, and so forth. Once in their sport groups, say “Audience position!” and give students 2 minutes to share with the class why they chose that sport as one of their favorites.

Follow the Leader

Explain to students that they are now ready for a different kind of warm-up where they get to be the leader!

Begin by teaching the procedure:

  1. Arrange students in window formation. Teacher stands at the front of the group.
  2. The teacher demonstrates a simple stretch or warm-up movement that students follow.
  3. The teacher will then walk behind a student and tap them gently on the shoulder.
  4. Once tapped, the student will move to the front of the room, and the teacher will stand in the student’s position in window formation.
  5. The student in front will lead the group in a new stretch or warm-up movement. Students follow.
  6. The teacher will then tap the shoulder of another student who will go to the front of the room, high-five the current student leader to switch spots, and lead the class in another new movement.
  7. The student in front returns to their original spot in the window formation.
  8. The teacher continues to tap on students to take turns leading the warm-up.

Warm-Up Guidelines

Explain to students that there are a few ways to make their turn as leader successful. “The purpose of a warm-up is to safely prepare our body and mind for dance. This means that any move you do must be safe and possible for all dancers in the room (ie. don’t go into the splits, just because you can – that is not a move that everyone can do safely or at all!).” Next, remind them that in order to warm up the body evenly, any stretch or move that you do on one side of the body, you must also do on the other side. Lastly, if you can’t think of a move to do, roll your wrists in a circle while you think of a move. Model.

  • Basketball
  • Ice Skating
  • Frisbee
  • Swimming
  • Football
  • Soccer

Encourage students to explore using all parts of their body including arm movement, legs, head/neck, spine/posture, etc.

After each sport, pause briefly to reflect on movements that stood out to you. Have students “silent shake” if they agree. Ask: “Raise your hand if you would like to compliment another student who you saw making creative and strong choices, those who took risks, and those who committed fully to the activity.”

Lesson Purpose

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What are some feelings that we might be able to show when performing our dance as a group?” Think of all the feelings we have been showing with our bodies and movement. Call on several students to respond. Then ask, “Please say a feeling you can show with fast music!” Allow students to freely respond. Then ask, “What about feelings we show when we dance to slow music?”

",,"
One Word/One Gesture
Ask students, “Who can tell us what the word ‘gesture’ means? Can you give me a few examples of gestures?” Share 3-5 examples from students.

Then, have each student take a few moments to silently think about one word that describes how they are feeling today. Remind them that today may be a different feeling than in the previous class! Go around the circle inviting each student to share their one-word feeling. After they share the word, everyone else in the circle will respond with a gesture that reflects that feeling. For example, if a student shares the word “tired,” the class might respond with a sleepy stretch, or folding their hands next to their face in a sleeping position. Repeat until all students have had a turn to share their one-word feeling.

,

Rollercoaster Breathing

Hold one hand open out in front of you, fingers stretched wide, use the other hand as a pointer finger and place your finger below your thumb knuckle on the opposite hand. As you trace your finger up the outside of your thumb, take a deep breath in and imagine you are on a rollercoaster, slowly making your way to the top. Then, trace your thumb down the other side, breathing out in a silent “scream” as you go down the rollercoaster. Repeat on each finger for 5 full breaths. Then, switch hands.

Flower/Candle Breathing

Hold one hand in a fist (as if holding a single flower stem) and the other hand with your pointer finger facing up (to represent a single candle). As you breathe in, hold the flower hand up to your nose, imagining you are smelling the flower; then breathe out, blowing the finger of the other hand as if blowing out a candle. Repeat 3-5 times.

Lion’s Breath

This is a breathing technique that allows you to breathe out any unwanted feelings to let them go. Imagine you are a mighty lion and sit up tall; breathe in and think about the feelings you want to release. As you breathe out, open your mouth as wide as possible (like a silent lion roar), stick out your tongue, and let out all the unwanted feelings. Repeat 3-5 times.

Wake Up/Goodnight Toes

(Variation on Hello/Goodbye Toes) “Remember ‘Hello Toes, Goodbye Toes’ that we did before? Here is another way to stretch our feet for dancing.” Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Wake up, toes!” followed by pointing the feet, and saying, “Goodnight, toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. While stretching, ask students how their body feels when it is awake and energized vs. tired and relaxed.

Butterfly Breathing

Sit tall with knees folded in butterfly position, hands holding the top of your ankles. Breathe in. As you breathe out, round the back, gently stretch the head forward, and slowly round forward toward the toes, using your arms to pull your torso toward your ankles and increase the stretch. As you breathe in, lengthen the spine and stretch forward and up, returning to sit tall. Repeat 3-5 breaths and then reverse direction, leaning forward with a lengthened spine, rounding through and back as you return to a seated position.

Sillies Shake-Out (Countdown)

Stand in Dancer Position and begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1. Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Mountain Pose

Regain focus by standing tall, feet shoulder width apart, arms long by your sides, palms open and facing forward. Imagine planting your feet into the ground while simultaneously lifting the crown of your head in opposition toward the sky. Take 3 breaths in this grounded yet lifted pose. On the next inhale, reach the arms out to the side and up over head, allowing your chin to lift and your gaze to shift upward towards your hands. On the exhale, open the arms wide and roll down, coming into a forward fold. Inhale as you lift up and repeat.

Favorite Color

Ask students, “What is one of your favorite colors?” Allow each student to quickly go around the circle sharing their response. Then, arrange the students in groups based on their color choice. For example, place all the students who chose red as their favorite color in a group, blue in a separate group, and so forth. Once they are in their color groups, give students 2 minutes to share why they chose that color as one of their favorites.

,

Point/Flex Toes (Color Variation)

“Audience Position!” Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Instruct students to flex and point their feet if they are wearing...red, blue, green, white, etc.

Finish by having all students bend the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet.

Butterfly Trip

Sit tall with legs in butterfly position, hands resting on top of the ankles. Tell students that we are going to fly somewhere that is blue. Ask students where we might fly to find blue (sky, ocean). Change colors as you go: Green (park), White (clouds), etc. Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and put on their brakes, making a quiet, squeaky brake sound.

Paint the Rainbow

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape, arms stretched out to each side. Explain that you are now going to paint all of the colors of the rainbow using our arms and hands as the paintbrush. Ask students, “What is the first color in the rainbow?” Then paint “red” by sweeping one arm up and over the body to meet the other arm, and lean over to one side. Holding that side stretch position, ask what the next color should be, and paint “orange” by reversing the direction of the arm sweep to arrive at the other side. Continue through all 6 colors of the rainbow: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple.

Color Countdown

Begin with students standing in Dancer Position. Explain that you will lift one arm overhead and shake it while saying the 6 colors of the rainbow, “Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Purple!” Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while repeating the 6 colors. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time saying the colors of the rainbow. Finally, shake your whole body and repeat the colors. All students should be saying the colors aloud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), saying one less color each time. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time, saying, “Red!” Finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Hello/Goodbye Toes

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Ask, “What is the opposite of hello?” Allow students to call-out, “Goodbye.” Then ask, “What is the opposite of flexing our toes?” Allow students to respond, “Pointing our toes.” Then begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello toes!” followed by pointing the feet, and saying, “Goodbye toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Dizzy Circle Toes

Remain seated with the legs extended straight out in front of the body. Circle the ankles/feet, and ask the students to identify if the feet are moving in the same or opposite direction; then, reverse direction. Challenge students to try moving both feet in the same direction and then opposite.

Butterfly Trip (Fast/Slow)

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be real or fictional) and if they would like to fly fast or slow. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and put on their brakes, making a quiet, squeaky brake sound.

No Talking: this is about exploring with your body, not your voice. (A little laughter is inevitable and totally ok.)

No Touching: this means that you should not touch any other dancer or anything else in the room (such as desks, chairs, things on the wall, etc.)

No Lying, Sitting, or Kneeling on the Floor: bodies need to stay standing for this exercise to ensure that no fingers or other body parts get stepped on, and no one accidentally trips over another dancer.

*If you have a large group, this activity can be done in 2 groups with the other group watching off to the side of the dance space.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What does a dancer do if they are feeling frustrated or upset by something, but have to perform a dance that is supposed to be happy and cheerful?” Allow 3-5 students to respond. Then explain that dancers also have to be actors, which means they learn to act out certain emotions required for the dance, even if that is not the emotion they are feeling inside.

",,"
One Word/One Gesture
Ask students, “Who remembers what the word ‘gesture’ means from our previous class? Can you give me a few examples?” Share 3-5 examples from students.

Then, have each student take a few moments to silently think about one word that describes how they are feeling today. Remind them that today may be a different feeling than in the previous class! Go around the circle inviting each student to share their one-word feeling. After they share the word, everyone else in the circle will respond with a gesture that reflects that feeling. For example, if a student shares the word “tired,” the class might respond with a sleepy stretch, or folding their hands next to their face in a sleeping position. Repeat until all students have had a turn to share their one-word feeling.

,

Butterfly Breathing

Sit tall with knees folded in butterfly position, hands holding the top of your ankles. Breathe in. As you breathe out, round the back, gently stretch the head forward, and slowly round forward toward the toes, using your arms to pull your torso toward your ankles and increase the stretch. As you breathe in, lengthen the spine and stretch forward and up, returning to sit tall. Repeat 3-5 breaths and then reverse direction, leaning forward with a lengthened spine, rounding through and back as you return to a seated position.

Mountain Pose

Stand tall, feet shoulder width apart, arms long by your sides, palms open and facing forward. Imagine planting your feet into the ground while simultaneously lifting the crown of your head in opposition toward the sky. Take 3 breaths in this grounded yet lifted pose. On the next inhale, reach the arms out to the side and up over head, allowing your chin to lift and your gaze shift upward towards your hands. On the exhale, open the arms wide and roll down, coming into a forward fold. Inhale as you lift up and repeat. <>

column1: Social-Emotional Learning: After repeating 2-3 times, ask students to hold the mountain pose and ask them how this makes them feel.

Bake a Pie

(Variation on Make a Pizza) Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to bake a pie! Begin by asking students what we will need first for the pie (crust). Shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (filling, topping, etc.). You can ask students for individual fillings and place them inside the imaginary crust, getting a forward stretch each time.

Now it is time for the pie to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pie inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pie to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pie knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pie is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pie out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch), eat the other side, and then eat all the pie in the middle, keeping legs as straight as possible.

“Today we get to show our emotions by being a grumpy bear, a sneaky monster, and a happy child! We are only going to be using our bodies for these movements, not our voices, remember! Let’s start!”

I will give you a few examples of gestures.” Demonstrate waving your hand in greeting, stretching as if tired, and crossing your arms with a frown as if mad. Explain that a gesture is movement without words that communicates an idea or feeling.

Have each student take a few moments to silently think about one word that describes how they are feeling today. Then, go around the circle inviting each student to share their one-word feeling. After they share the word, everyone else in the circle will respond with a gesture that reflects that feeling. For example, if a student shares the word “tired,” the class might respond with a sleepy stretch, or folding their hands next to their face in a sleeping position. Repeat until all students have had a turn to share their one-word feeling.

,

Rollercoaster Breathing

Explain to students, “The next few breathing activities will help our lungs work better when we dance. They will also help us feel calm and focused.” Model each breathing variation, and then have students repeat.

Hold one hand open out in front of you, fingers stretched wide; use the other hand as a pointer finger and place your finger below the thumb knuckle on the opposite hand.

As you trace your finger up the outside of your thumb, take a deep breath in and imagine you are on a rollercoaster, slowly making your way to the top. Then, trace your thumb down the other side, breathing out in a silent “scream” as you go down the rollercoaster. Repeat on each finger for 5 full breaths. Then, switch hands.

Flower/Candle Breathing

Hold one hand in a fist (as if holding a single flower stem) and the other hand with your pointer finger facing up (to represent a single candle). As you breathe in, hold the flower hand up to your nose, imagining you are smelling the flower; then breathe out, blowing the finger of the other hand, as if blowing out a candle. Repeat 3-5 times.

Lion’s Breath

This is a breathing technique that allows you to breathe out any unwanted feelings to let them go. Imagine you are a mighty lion and sit up tall; breathe in and think about the feelings you want to release. As you breathe out, open your mouth as wide as possible (like a silent lion roar), stick out your tongue, and let out all the unwanted feelings. Repeat 3-5 times.

Mountain Pose

Stand tall, feet shoulder width apart, arms long by your sides, palms open and facing forward. Imagine planting your feet into the ground while simultaneously lifting the crown of your head in opposition toward the sky. Take 3 breaths in this grounded yet lifted pose. On the next inhale, reach the arms out to the side and up over head, allowing your chin to lift and your gaze to shift upward towards your hands. On the exhale, open the arms wide and bend forward, coming into a forward fold. Inhale as you lift up and repeat. <>

column1: Social-Emotional Learning: After repeating 2-3 times, ask students to hold the mountain pose and ask them how this makes them feel.

<>

Wake Up/Goodnight Toes

(Variation on Hello/Goodbye Toes) Ask students, “Remember ‘Hello Toes, Goodbye Toes’ that we did before? Here is another way to stretch our feet for dancing.” Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet, and saying, “Wake up toes!” followed by pointing the feet, and saying, “Goodnight toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. While stretching, ask students how their body feels when it is awake and energized vs. tired and relaxed.

","

Feel the Moves

“Today we are going to combine movement with feelings or emotions. Sometimes we show how we are feeling by telling people. (‘I’m feeling happy!’) Sometimes we show our emotions by crying or laughing. Today we are just going to use our bodies and movement to show our feelings; no voices or sounds.”

Proud Jumps: Ask students, “What does it mean to feel ‘proud’?” Invite 2-3 students to respond. “How could we show ‘proud’ in our bodies, without using words?”

Then model a star jump (or jumping jack); when you jump out, feel like you are bursting with pride. When you jump back together, gather your energy and recharge for the next jump. This should be a big movement, but with control. Practice 8-10 proud star jumps as a group.

Excited Knees: “Now we are going to move as if we are really excited.” Begin in Dancer Position and demonstrate alternating high-knee jumps. Elbows will bend at your sides, forearms forward, hands extended, palms down. As you jump from one foot to the other, lift the opposite knee high in the air, trying to tap the palm of your hand to your knee. Challenge the students to see how controlled they can keep their upper body and how quiet they can make the jumps.

Scared Tiptoe: Allow students to move around the designated floor space without talking or touching (furniture or other dancers). Ask them to walk on their tiptoes as if they are sneaking away from a scary monster without being discovered. Encourage them to think about their whole body, not just their feet, as they move through the space expressing a scared emotion.

Ask students, “Who can name the emotion we felt doing the Proud Jump activity?” Call on several students (proud, strong, like a hero). Then ask, “Who can name the emotion we felt doing the Excited Knee activity?” (excited, energized, happy, free). Then ask, “Who can name the emotion we felt doing the Scared Tiptoe activity?” (afraid, scared, worried)

Begin by placing students in window formation. Review the choreography from the previous classes and practice and repeat movements as necessary. Remember to switch lines periodically to ensure all students can see the teacher from the front row. Continue to teach the next two to four 8-counts of choreography and add on to the previous steps.

*Choreography and song choice is at the discretion of the teacher. The choreography for this dance should be animal-themed and include elements of the steps and body positions students have learned in the preceding classes.

",,"

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

Ask students, “What was it like to express your feelings with movement instead of words?” Invite 3-5 students to share, encouraging a silent shake* response from the rest of the class if they are in agreement.

<>
“Silent Shake” is the hand sign for applause in ASL and is created by holding your hands in the air and twisting them back and forth.

Bows

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

To finish, ask students to gather their shoes and bring them back to the seated circle on the floor, the same way you began class. Instruct them to put their shoes back on, sit quietly, and place one hand on top of their head. When you see that they are ready, place a sticker on the hand that is resting on their head.

Circle-Up

High/Low Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. Instead of showing me with your thumb scale, I want you to show me with your whole body.” Demonstrate that standing tall (high) shows that you are feeling great and crouching low shows that they are not feeling great (low). Lesson Purpose

Assess Prior Knowledge

Such as, “What is the opposite of [fast, low, left, backwards, straight]?” Invite students to call out the answers (no raised hands needed) after each question.

Arrange students in window formation. Explain the rules of the game: “I am going to call out different directions that I would like you to follow. However, I only want you to follow the directions if you first hear me say, ‘Simon Says.’ If you don’t hear those words, continue doing what you were doing in the previous direction. For example, if you hear me say, ‘Simon says reach high up to the sky,’ you should all reach up high. But if my next instruction is, ‘Touch your toes,’ you should keep reaching up to the sky, because I didn’t say, ‘Simon Says’.”

Hello/Goodbye Toes

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Ask, “What is the opposite of hello?” Allow students to call-out, “Goodbye.” Then ask, “What is the opposite of flexing our toes?” Allow students to respond, “Pointing our toes.” Then begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello toes!” followed by pointing the feet, and saying, “Goodbye toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Dizzy Circle Toes

Remain seated with the legs extended straight out in front of the body. Circle the ankles/feet, and ask the students to identify if the feet are moving in the same or opposite direction; then, reverse direction. Challenge students to try moving both feet in the same direction and then opposite.

Butterfly Trip (Fast/Slow)

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be real or fictional) and if they would like to fly fast or slow. Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination in a fast or slow motion. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and put on their brakes, making a quiet, squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Head Isolations

Have students identify different ways they can move their head/neck to create opposites: right/left, up/down, side/side, circle one direction, then the other, etc.

Shoulder Isolations

Similar to the head, explore different ways to move the shoulders: up/down, right/left, circles both directions, forward/back, fast/slow.

Arm Circles

Move arms in a large circle forward/backward. For an added challenge, ask students to see if they can circle one arm forward and the other arm back, at the same time.

Obstacle Course (Procedure)

To set up this activity, create two parallel courses in the open floor space so that 2 students can move through the course at a time. Designate the starting line with a cone or poly dot. Introduce, demonstrate and practice each element individually, then combine into an obstacle course where each element is linked to the next.

Hoop Hops: Place 5 hula hoops on the floor in a row and have students jump into each one with both feet, hands on hips, careful not to touch the hoops or lose their balance. Explain that they need to think about the distance between each hoop, so that they don’t land on the hoop or outside of it.

Over the river: Place a large blue scarf or towel on the floor and explain to the students that the scarf represents a river, and they are going to jump over the “river.” Instruct them not to step in the river (touch the scarf), and try to help them leap with one foot extending out in front and landing on the same front foot (like a grande jeté). Explain that they need to use extra energy to get over the “river,” because it is further than just an ordinary step.

Side Chassé: Explain to students that, after the leap over the river, they will return to Start in a chassé step. With hands on hips or straight out to the side, step to the side with one foot, bring the other foot to meet it, then step out again with the original foot. The verbal cue is, “step together step.” Demonstrate and model. Explain that it is as if the second foot is chasing the first foot. As this is a traveling movement, the students should be light on their feet, lifted and gliding as they chassé across the floor. Students will chassé around the outside of the course, back to the end of the line and wait for their next turn. Have one student model for the class.

Ask students, “Raise a hand and tell us how it feels to return to the line doing the chassé step? Do you feel like you are moving faster or slower than just walking?” Explain that the chassé step helps us move faster because we are using more energy to progress forward.

Circle-Up

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. If you are having a great day, give me a thumbs up. If you are not having a good day, give me a thumbs down. And if it is somewhere in the middle, that is great too! OK, show me your thumb scale!” Briefly acknowledge each student’s level with a neutral, appreciative response.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will explore how to travel like different animals so that we can represent it as a dance.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Who can describe a way that an animal travels/moves from one spot to another? Humans walk or run to get from one place to another. Today, think about how animals move.” Allow 3-5 students to respond, encouraging them to think about flying, swimming, scurrying, slithering, hopping, etc.

column4: Favorite Animal (Animal Style)

Arrange students standing in a circle. Ask them to think back to their favorite dance move they did in the previous lessons. This time, see if they can perform their favorite move in the style of their favorite animal from the previous lesson. For example, if a student’s favorite animal is a cat, and their move involves a spin and a pose, how might a cat do the spin and pose? Model a few examples, and then rotate around the circle giving each student a turn.

,

Open the Bunny Gate

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Explain that your feet are going to create a gate and your hand is going to create a bunny that is trying to get through the gate. Begin by flexing the feet to make the walls of the gate and and making a “bunny” using two fingers as the ears.

To open the gate, keep the feet flexed but turn out the toes into a V-shape. “Hop” the bunny hand forward toward the gate as you fold forward with the body, keeping the legs straight in order to stretch the back of the legs. Reach the “bunny” arm forward as far as you can stretch, then close the gate (bringing feet back together, flexed and parallel) and sit up tall, pulling the bunny back. Repeat 5-8 times, alternating hands to be the bunny.

Spider Splits

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Pretend your fingers have turned into spiders. “Crawl” the spider hands down each leg, pausing to feel the stretch in the back of each leg. Then, crawl the spider hands forward as far as possible, getting a center stretch by folding the body forward and keeping the legs stretched straight out to the sides.

Cat/Cow

Have students come onto their hands and knees, making their backs flat like a table. Walk around the group seeing if you can place an imaginary glass of water on their backs without it falling off. Then cue students to stretch their backs up to the ceiling, pulling their belly button in towards their spine, rounding their back like a Halloween Cat, and have them say, “Meow.” Then slowly come back to the table-top position and extend your tummy down toward the ground, arching like the swayed-back of a cow, and say, “Moo!” Repeat 4-6 times.

Downward Facing Dog

From hands and knees position, have students push into their hands and lift their knees off the ground until the legs straighten and their body is forming an upside-down “V”. Cue them to try and lengthen through their arms, spine, and legs while saying “Ruff, Ruff!” like a dog.

","

Across the Floor

Mark a starting and ending dot or cone for 3 courses across the floor. Review the procedure to line up and move across in three lines. In this variation, students will improvise traveling movements in the style of various animals to move from one side of the room to the other. “Thumbs up if you understand dancers should stay on their feet. No crawling or rolling on the floor.”

Model each variation as you teach it.

Bunny Hops (Two-Feet Jump): Glue the inside of the legs together, stand tall, hands on hips, eyes looking forward. Jump up and forward with both legs, keeping legs squeezing tightly together and feet pointed in the air. Continue to jump across the floor, like a bunny, until you reach the cone at the opposite side. Try to keep the upper body lifted through the chest, remaining as still and controlled as possible, with quiet feet. Hands can be folded in bunny paws.

Frog Jumps: Begin in a deep squat with knees pointing out, heels lifted, arms touching the floor in front of your body. Jump up off the floor and slightly forward, trying to get all the way up in the air so that you can fully extend your legs. Land gently and quietly in the same position you started. Option to add a “Ribbit!” sound while jumping like a frog.

Flamingo Steps (Passé walks): Keeping feet flat, step forward and place one leg in parallel passé (as in the high knees variation). Teach students this position by getting out your “jar of glue” and brushing some glue onto the inside of the knee where your opposite foot can now “stick.” Each time they come into passé, they should glue the inside of their pointed foot to the inside of the opposite knee. Keep hands on hips, walking across the floor, lifting alternating feet into passé for each step.

Focus on tall posture, eyes looking forward (not down at floor), and keeping upper-body controlled and still as the lower half moves. Students can advance to walking in relevé (on tiptoe) as well, once balance and body control have been established. For flamingo variation, keep the neck long and fold arms into bird wings.

Horse Gallop (Side Chassé): With hands “holding the horse reigns,” begin by standing at the cone, facing the front of the room with your toe/leg pointed in the direction of the cone at the other side of the room. Keeping chest lifted and standing tall, step out onto the foot, bring the second foot to meet the first foot, then step out again on the first foot. Cue, “step, together, step.” Once this combination of steps is established, progress to a small jump in the air as the feet come together in the middle of the step, traveling across the floor. Repeat with the other foot leading on the other side.

Explain to students that the word “chassé” means “to chase” in French – so it is as if your second foot is chasing the front foot. As each student chassés across the floor, the rest of the class can make a 3-count gallop rhythm by clapping once and then tapping their legs right/left, repeating at a quick tempo.

Crab Walks: Begin by lowering the body to the ground, placing your hands on the ground with your arms extended behind you, fingers pointed in toward your feet. Lift hips off the ground in an “inverted tabletop” position, and walk across the floor on your hands and feet.

Shape Breathing

Seated in a circle, “Audience Position!,” legs crossed, spine tall, explain that you are going to breathe, using shapes as your guide.

  • Square: Instruct students to trace a square shape In the air with their finger, beginning at the top of the square. Inhale for 4 counts as you trace your finger along the top line of the imaginary square, then hold your breath for 4 counts as you trace the line down the side. Then exhale for 4 counts as you draw the bottom line, and hold your breath for 4 counts as you draw the final line up to close the shape. Demonstrate, then have students copy. Repeat 3-5 times.
  • Triangle: Begin at the bottom of the imaginary triangle shape and trace in the air the first side of the triangle, moving the finger up at an angle while inhaling for 3 counts. As you trace the second side of the triangle, hold the breath for 3 counts, complete the last side of the triangle by exhaling for 3 counts. Demonstrate, then have students copy. Repeat 3-5 times.
  • Lazy 8 / Infinity: Imagine the number 8, lying on its side (like the infinity symbol). Model the shape. Begin in the center of the 8 and trace the finger around one loop as you inhale for 4 counts, then continue moving the finger around the shape, exhaling for 4 counts as you trace the other loop. Repeat 3-5 times.
  • Circle: Use your finger to trace a circle shape in the air, beginning at the bottom, and moving up. Inhale as you trace the circle up and around, exhale as you continue to trace the circle down and around. Demonstrate, then students copy. The circle can start small with shorter breaths and then grow to make larger circles with longer breaths.

Remain seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the sides of their legs. Begin by flexing the feet and notice what kind of line the feet make (straight line), “like a tall building!” Then, point the feet towards the floor and notice the curved line, “like a bridge,” made by the pointed feet. Demonstrate and then have students repeat 4-6 times.

Diamond Butterfly Stretch

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will explore the movement qualities of different animals in order to discover new ways to move the body.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Raise a quiet hand if you can name an animal we can pretend to be as dancers?” Call on 3-5 students. Then ask, “Is there any type of animal we cannot create as dancers? Who can name one?” Then explain that with our bodies and imaginations, we can become any animal we choose!

",,"
Favorite Animal

Arrange students standing in a circle. To begin, explain that each student is going to have a turn to share their favorite animal. But because this is a dance class, ask them to share their animal by silently moving like the animal and have the rest of the class try to guess with a quiet, raised hand.

“Show us with a thumb up or down if you are going to use your voice for this activity. Continue around the circle until each student has had a turn to share their favorite animal with silent movement.

,

Open the Bunny Gate

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Explain that your feet are going to create a gate and your hand is going to create a bunny that is trying to get through the gate. Begin by flexing the feet to make the walls of the gate and and making a “bunny” using two fingers as the ears.

To open the gate, keep the feet flexed but turn out the toes into a V-shape. “Hop” the bunny hand forward toward the gate as you fold forward with the body, keeping the legs straight in order to stretch the back of the legs. Reach the “bunny” arm forward as far as you can stretch, then close the gate (bringing feet back together, flexed and parallel) and sit up tall, pulling the bunny back. Repeat 5-8 times, alternating hands to be the bunny.

Spider Splits

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Pretend your fingers have turned into spiders. “Crawl” the spider hands down each leg, pausing to feel the stretch in the back of each leg. Then, crawl the spider hands forward as far as possible, getting a center stretch by folding the body forward and keeping the legs stretched straight out to the sides.

Cat/Cow

Have students come onto their hands and knees, making their backs flat like a table. Walk around the group seeing if you can place an imaginary glass of water on their backs without it falling off. Then cue students to stretch their backs up to the ceiling, pulling their belly button in towards their spine, rounding their back like a Halloween Cat, and have them say, “Meow.” Then slowly come back to the table-top position and extend your tummy down toward the ground, arching like the swayed-back of a cow, and say, “Moo!” Repeat 4-6 times.

Downward Facing Dog

From hands and knees position, have students push into their hands and lift their knees off the ground until the legs straighten and their body is forming an upside-down “V”. Cue them to try and lengthen through their arms, spine, and legs while saying “Ruff, Ruff!” like a dog.

Invite students to stand up and spread out around the dance space, making sure they are not touching anyone, or too close to any furniture. Explain that they will now play a version of Freeze Dance. Review the steps of Freeze Dance for those who may not have played before: model and check for understanding.

  1. When the music begins, you start dancing.
  2. When the music stops, you Freeze!

Then tell students that the same rules apply for when we do free dance together. Ask, “Does anyone remember the three rules from our free dance?”

No Talking: this is about exploring dance with your body, not your voice. (A little laughter is inevitable and totally ok.)

No Touching: this means that you should not touch any other dancer or anything else in the room (such as desks, chairs, things on the wall, etc.)

No Dancing on the Floor: bodies need to stay standing for this exercise to ensure that no fingers or other body parts get stepped on and no one accidentally trips over another dancer.

In this version, there will be no competition or elimination rounds as you want to encourage student participation throughout the full activity. However, if a student cannot control their body when asked to freeze, you may need to remove them from the game temporarily until you and the student feel they can safely try again.

Circle-Up

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. If you are having a great day, give me a thumbs up. If you are not having a good day, give me a thumbs down. And if it is somewhere in the middle, that is great too! OK, show me your thumb scale!” Briefly acknowledge each student’s level with a neutral, appreciative response.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will begin learning their first choreographed dance. Each week they will review and add on new movements, until they have a full dance to share and perform!

Assess Prior Knowledge

column4: Animal Name
Arrange students standing in a circle. Ask them to think about the first letter in their name. Then ask them to think of an animal that starts with the same letter.

For example, if the student’s name is Karim, he might think of a Kangaroo! Once students have thought of an animal that starts with the same first letter as their name, ask them to go around the circle acting out the movement of the animal for the group. If students have chosen the same animal, encourage them to show a different way to move their body than the previous student(s).

,

Open the Bunny Gate

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Explain that your feet are going to create a gate and your hand is going to create a bunny that is trying to get through the gate. Begin by flexing the feet to make the walls of the gate and and making a “bunny” using two fingers as the ears.

To open the gate, keep the feet flexed but turn out the toes into a V-shape. “Hop” the bunny hand forward toward the gate as you fold forward with the body, keeping the legs straight in order to stretch the back of the legs. Reach the “bunny” arm forward as far as you can stretch, then close the gate (bringing feet back together, flexed and parallel) and sit up tall, pulling the bunny back. Repeat 5-8 times, alternating hands to be the bunny.

Spider Splits

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Pretend your fingers have turned into spiders. “Crawl” the spider hands down each leg, pausing to feel the stretch in the back of each leg. Then, crawl the spider hands forward as far as possible, getting a center stretch by folding the body forward and keeping the legs stretched straight out to the sides.

Cat/Cow

Have students come onto their hands and knees, making their backs flat like a table. Walk around the group seeing if you can place an imaginary glass of water on their backs without it falling off. Then cue students to stretch their backs up to the ceiling, pulling their belly button in towards their spine, rounding their back like a Halloween Cat, and have them say, “Meow.” Then slowly come back to the table-top position and extend your tummy down toward the ground, arching like the swayed-back of a cow, and say, “Moo!” Repeat 4-6 times.

Downward Facing Dog

From hands and knees position, have students push into their hands and lift their knees off the ground until the legs straighten and their body is forming an upside-down “V”. Cue them to try and lengthen through their arms, spine, and legs while saying “Ruff, Ruff!” like a dog.

Window Formation (Procedure)

Now you will teach them a new procedure for learning choreography. Place the students in lines with windows, using cones or poly dots as spacing guides.

Introduction to Choreography

Introduce students to choreography and how it compares to improvisation: unlike the dancing they have done so far (known as improvisation, where you create the movement on the spot), this dance will be created using choreography, where you learn specific steps that you will memorize with the music. Each week you will teach a bit more of the dance so that by the end, they have a full dance to share!

“Improvisation is when you make up your own dance moves. Everybody say, ‘improvisation!’ Choreography is when you all do the same, identical steps you are taught. Everyone say, ‘choreography!’.”

“Raise your hand if you’ve ever done the ‘Hokey-Pokey’ song where you put your arms in or out, and your legs in or out?” Model. “This is an example of a dance that has steps that everyone does together, not made up on your own.”

With students in window formation, teach the first four 8-counts of choreography to students, Practice and repeat movement.

*Choreography and song choice is at the discretion of the teacher. The choreography for this dance should be animal-themed and include elements of the steps and body positions students have learned in the preceding classes.

",,"

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

Ask students, “What is ‘choreography’?” Allow 2-3 students to respond. Then ask, “And who can tell me, what is ‘improvisation’?” Allow 2-3 different students to respond. Then say, “After I count to 3, let’s all say our favorite kind of dance: choreography or improvisation! 1-2-3...”

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer position.”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Remind the other students that they can use the “silent shake/applause” hand signal if a student shares the same book they were thinking of.

Then explain, “All stories need to have three things in order to be a story: a beginning, a middle, and an end.” Use one of the stories mentioned by students in the previous question as an example: identify the beginning, middle, and end of the sample story.

Dance Telephone

Arrange students evenly into 3 lines, front to back, standing in Dancer Position, and using the whole floor space so everyone has room to move. All students should be facing the same direction (toward the designated “back” of the room). Ask the first student in each of the 3 lines to turn and face the front (while everyone else remains facing the back).

Demonstrate a simple movement to the 3 starting students, and ask them to repeat the movement back to you to ensure they accurately copied the movement. Then have each of the three students turn around to face their line, tap the next student in line on the shoulder, cueing them to turn toward the front, and then demonstrate the exact same movement as closely as possible to what they saw originally. The student second in line will then tap the next student in line on the shoulder and repeat the movement as closely as possible.

Play continues down the line, similar to the game of telephone. When it gets to the end of the line, ask the final three students to make their way to the front of the room and ask all students to turn to face the front. Have each of the final three students demonstrate the movement they learned, and then compare it to the teacher’s original movement.
Ask students, “Did the movement change or did it remain close to the original? Why is it important for us to notice and repeat every detail as closely as possible?” Invite 3-5 students to respond.
