Intro

“Do you know the story of ‘The Very Hungry Caterpillar?’ The story tells us about a hungry caterpillar’s life, from ‘birth to butterfly’. As we warm-up our bodies to be ready to dance today, we are going to move like a caterpillar!”

For this warm-up, the movements will loosely follow the story of “The Very Hungry Caterpillar” by Eric Carle, exploring the progression from caterpillar, to chrysalis, to butterfly. In each exercise, demonstrate the new movement first, then have students follow.

Caterpillar Stretch (Cat/Cow)

Instruct students to think about how a caterpillar moves, inching, bending, and scooting to travel. Begin on hands and knees; demonstrate for students how to slowly bend the spine -- moving from an arched, rounded back to a concave arch in the reverse direction. The movement should feel continuous and rolling, like a caterpillar.

Growing Caterpillar (Down Dog/Cobra + Child’s Pose)

From hands and knees, push up to a downward facing dog position, arms and legs extended in an upside “V” shape. Move like a caterpillar smoothly from down dog into cobra, extending the chest up and open, then roll back into down dog. Roll through the two positions 3-5 times and then finish in child’s pose, pretending you are a caterpillar hiding from the birds above. Kneel on the ground, allowing your spine to round over your legs and fold forward.

Heel/Toe/Leg Stretch

Come to a seated position, grab heels or toes, walk legs out like a caterpillar inching forward (pretending to be a caterpillar finding food), then walk legs in (to hide from the birds). Repeat 4-6 times.

Food Splits

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Bend over each leg and eat imaginary food off the tops of each leg and all the food in the middle space created by the seated second split position. Ask students for suggestions for what type of food the caterpillar should eat.

Tree Pose

“Now let’s stand up and get into ‘Dancer Position’. Let’s pretend to find a tree in which to make your cocoon (tree pose). Raise your hand if you can tell us what a ‘cocoon’ is?” Invite 1-2 students to respond.

Begin by standing tall in mountain pose and lift one foot off the ground balancing on the standing leg. Bend the knee of the lifted leg and place the foot on the inside of the standing leg, either low at the ankle, or just above the knee. (The higher the foot is placed along the leg, the more challenging to balance; just ensure that students are not placing their foot directly on the knee joint). Place the arms out to the side to help balance and then lift arms up into “branches” of the tree. Hold the balance, then switch legs.

Cocoon

“Audience Position. Now let’s make our bodies into a cocoon.” Lay on your back in a tight ball, roll back and forth, massaging the spine. As an added challenge, start seated in the tight ball, balancing with the feet slightly off the ground. Roll back and then return to a seated position, trying not to let your feet touch the ground at any time. Demonstrate, then students copy.

Butterfly

“Now our cocoon will turn into a butterfly!” Remain in a seated position and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you have now become butterflies and get to fly to your first flower to find nectar. “Land” on the flower by gently pushing down on the tops of the knees for a stretch, bend forward and “drink” the nectar while getting a deeper stretch through the legs and spine.

The next three classes will focus on the story, “Giraffes Can’t Dance,” by Giles Andreae.

Intro

“Now we are going to move like another animal, the giraffe! Pay close attention as I read the book to you.” Before the video or reading starts, ask the students to listen and/or look for a dance move that they might be able to copy from the story.

Begin by reading the story aloud to students or watching the video version HERE. During the story, stop if it seems necessary to define key vocabulary words that students may not yet know. For example, when the giraffe, “buckles at the knees,” discuss what the verb “buckles” means and how that might look in your body. Explain that in upcoming classes, you will improvise movements that could be performed to tell this story, so it’s important that you understand Gerald the Giraffe’s moves!

“What were some of Gerald the Giraffes’s dance moves?” (hooves shuffled and made circles on the ground, his neck swayed, his tail swished, he threw his arms out and swung them, he did a backwards somersault) Call on students to share.

Ask students to identify the beginning, middle, and end of the story.

At the end of the book, Gerald says, “We all can dance when we find music that we love.” Do you think this is true for you? What music do you love that makes you want to dance?” Have 2-3 students respond.

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Lesson Purpose

Tell students, “Today we are going to use our bodies to create a story and bring it to life! Can anyone guess what story we are going to use? It starts with a ‘G’!”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Does anyone remember what happens at the beginning of the story, ‘Giraffes Can’t Dance?’ What happens in the middle? What happens at the end? What are some of your favorite stories?” Invite students to respond and review the three sections:

  1. Beginning — Gerald the giraffe is sad because he is bad at dancing.
  2. Middle — All the animals in Africa have a dance party and show off their moves. They laugh at Gerald when it is his turn, and tell him, “Giraffes can’t dance.”
  3. End — A friendly cricket helps Gerald realize that he CAN dance...he just needs to find the right music to help him. He performs happily for all his animal friends.

Dance Telephone

Arrange students evenly into 3 lines, front to back, standing in Dancer Position, and using the whole floor space so everyone has room to move. All students should be facing the same direction (toward the designated “back” of the room). Ask the first student in each of the 3 lines to turn and face the front (while everyone else remains facing the back).

In this variation, the teacher will demonstrate a different movement for each line. Show each line leader the move for their line, and ask them to repeat the movement back to you to ensure they accurately copied the movement. Then, have each of the three students turn around to face their line, tap the next student in line on the shoulder, cueing them to turn toward the front, and demonstrate the exact same movement as closely as possible to what they saw originally. The student second in line will then tap the next student in line on the shoulder and repeat the movement as closely as possible.

Play continues down the line, similar to the game of telephone. When it gets to the end of the line, ask the final three students to make their way to the front of the room, and ask all students to turn to face the front. Have each of the final three students demonstrate the movement they learned, and then compare it to the teacher’s original movement.
Ask students, “Did the movement change or did it remain close to the original?” Invite 3-5 students to respond.

For this warm-up, the movements will loosely follow the story of “The Very Hungry Caterpillar” by Eric Carle, exploring the progression from caterpillar, to chrysalis, to butterfly. In each exercise, demonstrate the new movement first, then have students follow.

Caterpillar Stretch (Cat/Cow)

Instruct students to think about how a caterpillar moves, inching, bending, and scooting to travel. Begin on hands and knees; demonstrate for students how to slowly bend the spine -- moving from an arched, rounded back to a concave arch in the reverse direction. The movement should feel continuous and rolling, like a caterpillar.

Growing Caterpillar (Down Dog/Cobra + Child’s Pose)

From hands and knees, push up to a downward facing dog position, arms and legs extended in an upside “V” shape. Move like a caterpillar smoothly from down dog into cobra, extending the chest up and open, then roll back into down dog. Roll through the two positions 3-5 times and then finish in child’s pose, pretending you are a caterpillar hiding from the birds above. Kneel on the ground, allowing your spine to round over your legs and fold forward.

Heel/Toe/Leg Stretch

Come to a seated position, grab heels or toes, walk legs out like a caterpillar inching forward (pretending to be a caterpillar finding food), then walk legs in (to hide from the birds). Repeat 4-6 times.

Food Splits

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Bend over each leg and eat imaginary food off the tops of each leg and all the food in the middle space created by the seated second split position. Ask students for suggestions for what type of food the caterpillar should eat.

Tree Pose

“Now let’s stand up and get into ‘Dancer Position’. Let’s pretend to find a tree in which to make your cocoon (tree pose). Raise your hand if you can tell us what a ‘cocoon’ is?” Invite 1-2 students to respond.

Begin by standing tall in mountain pose and lift one foot off the ground balancing on the standing leg. Bend the knee of the lifted leg and place the foot on the inside of the standing leg, either low at the ankle, or just above the knee. (The higher the foot is placed along the leg, the more challenging to balance; just ensure that students are not placing their foot directly on the knee joint). Place the arms out to the side to help balance and then lift arms up into “branches” of the tree. Hold the balance, then switch legs.

Cocoon

“Audience Position. Now let’s make our bodies into a cocoon.” Lay on your back in a tight ball, roll back and forth, massaging the spine. As an added challenge, start seated in the tight ball, balancing with the feet slightly off the ground. Roll back and then return to a seated position, trying not to let your feet touch the ground at any time. Demonstrate, then students copy.

Butterfly

“Now our cocoon will turn into a butterfly!” Remain in a seated position and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you have now become butterflies and get to fly to your first flower to find nectar. “Land” on the flower by gently pushing down on the tops of the knees for a stretch, bend forward and “drink” the nectar while getting a deeper stretch through the legs and spine.

Giraffes Can’t Dance (Improvised Story)

“At the start of class today we reviewed the beginning, middle and end of the story ‘Giraffes Can’t Dance.’ Now let’s retell the story, not with our words, but with our bodies through dancing.”

Begin by dividing the students into 3 groups and invite the first group onto the “stage.” Read the beginning of the story aloud (from the physical book), and have the first group move/act out each part of the story for the audience. Encourage students to use the text from the story combined with their imaginations to tell the story through their bodies and movement. Keep the structure of this activity loose: students can act out any character or element they choose! For example, there can be multiple dancers who choose to be the giraffe, or even dancers who choose to be an object, such as the tree or moon.

When you get to the middle of the story, switch to the second group of dancers to give them a turn to improvise this middle section of the story. Finish with the third group dancing the end section of the story. <>

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer Position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Hello/Goodbye Toes

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Begin seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Ask, “What is the opposite of hello?” Allow students to call-out, “Goodbye.” Then ask, “What is the opposite of flexing our toes?” Allow students to respond, “Pointing our toes.” Then begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello toes!” followed by pointing the feet, and saying, “Goodbye toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Dizzy Circle Toes

Remain seated with the legs extended straight out in front of the body. Circle the ankles/feet, and ask the students to identify if the feet are moving in the same or opposite direction; then, reverse direction. Challenge students to try moving both feet in the same direction and then opposite.

Butterfly Trip (Fast/Slow)

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be real or fictional) and if they would like to fly fast or slow. Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination in a fast or slow motion. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and put on their brakes, making a quiet, squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Head Isolations

Have students identify different ways they can move their head/neck to create opposites: right/left, up/down, side/side, circle one direction, then the other, etc.

Shoulder Isolations

Similar to the head, explore different ways to move the shoulders: up/down, right/left, circles both directions, forward/back, fast/slow.

Arm Circles

Move arms in a large circle forward/backward. For an added challenge, ask students to see if they can circle one arm forward and the other arm back, at the same time.

Obstacle Course (Procedure)

To set up this activity, create three parallel courses in the open floor space so that 3 students can move through the course at a time. Designate the starting line and the finish line with a cone or poly dot. Introduce and practice each element individually, then combine into an obstacle course where each element is linked to the next.

“Today we’re going to use opposites in the way we dance across the floor. Sometimes we will be walking on our toes, not our feet. Sometimes we will be walking backwards, not forwards. Sometimes we will be walking in a zigzag line, not a straight line. Let’s try it!”

Relevé Walks: Place a “ladder” of 8 artificial rose stems on the floor. Instruct students to rise onto their tip toes and step ‘en relevé’ over each rose, careful not to touch the thorny stems. Body stays tall and lifted. *Option to add a passé/high knee for a more advanced variation.

Heel/Toe Backward Walk: Take slow, careful steps backwards, touching toe to heel for each step from point A to point B (marked by cones or poly dots), hands on hips or out to side for balance.

Ask students, “Who can tell us, does it take you longer or shorter time to travel the same distance when walking backward, compared to the Relevé Walk on tiptoes?” Call on 2-3 students to respond.

Airplane Walk: Place 6 cones in a line, and instruct students to zigzag around each cone with arms out to the side like an airplane.

Ask students, “Think for a moment, then tell us, which step took the most energy: tiptoes, backwards or zigzag?” Pause while they think, then call on 2-3 students. Explain, “It takes more energy to do the Airplane Walk, because when you zigzag, you cover more distance and take more steps!”

Lesson Purpose

Assess Prior Knowledge

Review “Dancer” and “Audience Position.”

Dancer Position

“When I call out “Dancer Position!” that is your cue to stand up tall, feet together, knees pulled up straight, arms down by your sides (out of pockets or shirt sleeves). Head is lifted, shoulders down, eyes open, mouth closed. Body and eyes should be facing the teacher.” Model first, then have students practice this position all together and correct any student’s positions as needed.

Then tell them that you are going to practice this a few times to make sure they have it. When you say, “Be silly,” the students can move their bodies and talk in a silly way.

Model this so students keep hands and bodies from touching or bothering anybody else. When they hear you say, “Dancer Position!” they should immediately stop their movement and freeze in the correct position. Tell students you will be using this phrase, “Dancer Position!” at the start and during each activity so that they are ready to listen and learn.

Audience Position

Have students return to a seated position in a circle. “There will also be times in dance class where you will be seated as an audience, watching other students dance. When I call out ‘Audience Position!,’ what do you think that might look like?” Identify students who are modeling elements of the correct position. Have students sit cross-legged, spine lifted tall, and hands on top of their knees. Their eyes should be open, mouth closed, and they should be looking at the person speaking or the dancer(s) performing. “When you hear me say, ‘Audience Position!,’ you should immediately stop your movement and speaking, and get into that seated position.”

column4: Favorite Move

Arrange students standing in a circle. In this variation, point to a student in the circle to begin, and ask the rest of the class if they can say the student’s name and favorite move. If the class cannot remember, ask the student to remind them of the movement by demonstrating, then have the full class repeat the name and movement. Continue quickly around the circle until all students have shared their name and movement.

,

Hello/Goodbye Toes

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello toes!” followed by pointing the feet and saying, “Goodbye toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Finish by bending the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet. Lift the head up, trying to lengthen the spine and flex the feet saying, “Hello toes!” and then round the spine forward, nodding the head down and pointing the feet (keeping hands resting on the top of the foot/ankle) and say, “Goodbye toes.” Repeat 3-5 times.

Butterfly Trip

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be a real or pretend location). Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and “put on their brakes,” making a soft squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Make a Pizza

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to make a pretend pizza! Begin by asking, “What is the first thing we need to make a pizza?” Take 2-3 suggestions from students. Then say, “We need pizza dough!” Model and tell students to follow: shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (sauce, cheese, etc.). You can ask students for individual toppings and place them all around the imaginary pizza, getting a forward stretch each time. Remind students to try and keep their legs straight, “so their pizza stays flat and doesn’t get squished.”

Now it is time for the pizza to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pizza inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pizza to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pizza knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pizza is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pizza out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch), eat the other side, and then eat all the pizza in the middle, keeping legs as straight as possible.

Countdown

Bring all students to a standing position in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1.

Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

","

Across the Floor Procedure

Mark a starting and ending dot or cone for 3 courses across the floor. Review the procedure to line up and move across in three lines. In this variation, students will improvise movement in the style of suggested characters and animals as they dance from one side of the room to the other. CFU: Remind students about safety: they need to stay on their feet. No crawling or rolling on the floor.

Like a Robot: Tell students, “First I would like you to move like a robot. Think about the stiff, jerky movements they have, and try to make all parts of your body move in that style, not just your arms. Think about your head, your legs, AND your arm movement.” Model and CFU.

Like a Spider: “Now I want you to dance across the floor like a spider. Think about all of their legs, their quick crawling movement, and their small size.” Have students move across the floor like a spider.

Like a Giant: “Now I want you to be a giant. Try to make your movements big, slow, and heavy (without being loud).” Have students move across the floor like a giant.

Like a Mermaid: “How would you move if you were a mermaid? Explore different ways you can move your body as if underwater. Try to make your movement smooth and fluid.” Have students move across the floor like a mermaid.

",,"

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

Ask students, “What was your favorite character to explore through dance?” Allow 6-8 students to respond.

","

Bows

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

To finish, ask students to gather their shoes and bring them back to the seated circle on the floor, the same way you began class. Instruct them to put their shoes back on, sit quietly, and place one hand on top of their head. When you see that they are ready, place a sticker on the hand that is resting on their head.

Circle-Up

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. OK, show me your thumb scale!” Briefly acknowledge each student’s level with a neutral, appreciative response.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students, “In the last classes we learned about dance in Africa and Mexico. Today we are going to travel in our imaginations to another country, India, to learn about the dance styles in that culture.”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Raise your hand if you have heard of the country of India? Do you know anyone from India? Have you ever seen or performed dance from India before? What do you know about this dance style?” Invite 3-5 students to respond.

Seven Jumps:

Begin by standing in a circle in Dancer Position. Share with students that the next activity is from a popular folk song and dance originating in Denmark, a country in Europe, called, “The Seven Jumps.” It is danced to the folk song of the same name performed by Shenanigans.
Intro

The song begins with a series of three sustained chords, students will listen to these chords as they prepare for the first movement section. Play the first notes of the song, and ask students to “Nod your head if you hear these three chords.”
Chorus

Gently hold hands in the circle and begin walking (or skipping) as a group, all going in the same direction for 8 counts. After 8 counts, stomp your feet 3 times, clap your hands 3 times, stomp feet again 3 times, and clap hands again 3 times.
*This chorus section of music and movement will repeat after each verse.
Verse 1: Lift the right foot up when the high note plays and place the foot on the ground when the second, lower note plays. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 2: Lift the right foot up when the first note plays and place the foot on the ground with the lower note. Then lift the left foot up as the high note repeats, and place the left foot on the ground with the lower note. (Repeat chorus section)
Verse 3: Repeat the right foot and left foot, then lift the right knee up and gently kneel, placing the right knee on the floor. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 4: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee and then lift left knee and place on floor so that you are now kneeling on both knees. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle again for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 5: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, and then lift the right elbow toward the sky and gently place it on the ground. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 6: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right elbow, and then lift left elbow and place on the floor. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 7: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right elbow, left elbow, and then gently place the head on the floor. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

For this warm-up, explain to students that they will be learning different movements and styles of dance from around the world. It is recommended to choose music that supports each warm-up genre or use the playlist provided.

Ballet (France)

Pliés — begin by standing tall in first position, feet in a turned out V, hands on your hips. Keeping the spine long, bend the knees as deeply as possible without the heels lifting off the ground. Repeat 6-8 times. *Can add arms in first position if student level allows. Continue the same exercise with feet wide in second position. When bending the knees, remind students to stay lifted in the spine and not to bend forward or stick hips back.

Tendues ­— begin in first position, hands on hips. Slide one foot forward until fully extended in a pointed position, keeping knees straight. Slide foot back to starting position. Repeat 6-8 times on one leg and then switch sides. Continue with tendues to the side and back on each leg.

Latin Dance

Hip/Torso Isolations — begin by standing tall, feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hands on your hips. Shift the hips from right to left, trying to keep the rest of the body still and controlled. Repeat right to left for 8 counts. Transition to shifting hips forward and back for 8 counts, with the rest of the body remaining still. Then move into combining all 4 directions (front, side, back, side) in both directions. After completing the hip isolations, repeat the entire sequence with the torso.

African Dance

Shoulder Isolations­ — stay in the standing posture (feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hands on your hips) and isolate the shoulders by lifting them up toward the ears, center/neutral, and then down toward the floor. The sequence will be “up, center, down, center.” Then remove the “center” position and alternate between shoulders going “up, down, up, down.” This can eventually be sped up to double speed. Repeat both sequences 6-8 times. Variations of this sequence can include alternating one shoulder at a time, rolling shoulders forward and back, etc.

Head/Neck Isolations — Following a similar pattern to the shoulder isolations, begin by rotating the neck side to side in the pattern, “right, center, left, center.” After repeating 4 times on each side, remove the pause in the center position, and simply look from side to side, on the beat. Repeat side to side 8 times. Continue this sequence with the head tilting side to side, keeping shoulders down, reaching right ear to right shoulder, center, and then left ear to left shoulder, and back to center. Repeat 4 times on each side, take out the center position and tilt right to left 8 times. Lastly, repeat the whole sequence isolating the head forward and back. Finish by rolling the neck in a slow circle, 2-4 times each direction, careful to keep the neck long and lengthened, so as not to stretch the neck too far in any single position.

Contemporary Dance (United States)

Fluid Stretch Flow - begin in second position, toes and knees gently turned out. Arms open wide to second position, and bend knees into deep grand plié, reminding students (just like in the ballet plié) to keep the spine lifted and keep hips under shoulders, as if you were squatting with your back against a wall. Repeat for 4 pliés. Keeping legs in second position, knees straight, move into a side stretch with the torso leaning to the right, left arm reaching up and overhead. Continue to a flat back stretch, swooping the right arm down by your side, while the left arm stays stretched overhead. Rotate the torso so the chest is facing the floor, trying to create a “tabletop” with your back, parallel to the floor, knees stay soft but not bent. Continue the stretch by folding forward over your right leg, nose toward the knee. Keeping the body folded forward, move the torso towards the middle, centered between both legs, before rolling up and repeating on the other side. Each of the 4 positions in this stretch can be introduced for a hold of 8 counts in each position, and then shortened to 4 counts each. Repeat the sequence on both sides 2-4 times.

Hip-Hop (United States)

Up/Down Bounce — Begin standing with feet hip distance apart, knees soft and bent, for the down bounce. Listening to the beat of the music, bend the knees to the beat and let your whole body “bounce” with the emphasis being down towards the ground. Keep the upper body loose and free, letting it add to the down bounce of the legs. Continue for 4 8-counts of music. *Option to add a small step, alternating feet, as the bounce continues. Transition to an up bounce where the knees will lengthen to a straight position (without locking or hyperextending the knees) and the rest of the body will lift, emphasizing the bounce on the “up” motion. Continue with the up bounce for 4 8-counts.

Freestyle — From the bounces, invite students to see where their bounce may lead. Let them groove to the music, explaining to them that in hip-hop, this is called “freestyle,” where you are free to show off your own unique style and dance in any way that makes you feel confident and happy. Remind students to respect other bodies while moving their own.

Indian Dance

Begin by telling students, “Now we are going to travel to a different country in the world, one that is far from away from all the other places we have learned about so far. India! In India, there are certain dances that are traditionally performed for the wealthy, or upper-class members of a community, and performed in fancy palaces. These dances often tell stories from India’s history, and have lavish costumes and jewelry. You will also find dancing in the less wealthy communities; these are known as folk dances. Similar to the Folklórico dance of Mexico, these folk dances represent the unique cultures in various regions across India.”

“Just like we did with Africa and Mexico, today we will watch a video of a dance from India. Again, as you watch, look for shapes, colors and feelings represented!”

Show students a video example of kids performing Indian dance. (Below you will find a list of suggested clips). As students are watching, ask them to think about the following three questions:

  1. What types of shapes do you see them making with their bodies?
  2. What types of colors do you see represented in the dance?
  3. What feelings are they expressing?

Begin by placing students in window formation. Review the choreography from the previous classes and practice and repeat movements as necessary. Remember to switch lines periodically to ensure all students can see the teacher from the front row.

Then, divide the class into two groups, designating one as the audience and one as the performing group. Remind students of Audience Position, and ask them to observe their classmates attentively, noticing particular movements or styles that stand out in a positive way. After each performance, allow students to share elements they observed and liked, prompting them to use specific dance vocabulary, if possible. Then switch groups.

Ask students, “Let’s compare the dances of Africa, Mexico, and India. How are they alike, and how are they different?” Invite 4-6 students to respond as a group.

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer Position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

Lesson Purpose

Has anyone here seen it or danced in this style before?” Invite 3-5 students to respond. “Later in our lesson we will watch a video of children doing Folklórico dance!”

Seven Jumps:

Begin by standing in a circle in Dancer Position. Share with students that the next activity is from a popular folk song and dance originating in Denmark, a country in Europe, called, “The Seven Jumps.” It is danced to the folk song of the same name performed by Shenanigans.
Intro

The song begins with a series of three sustained chords, students will listen to these chords as they prepare for the first movement section. Play the first notes of the song, and ask students to “Nod your head if you hear these three chords.”
Chorus

Gently hold hands in the circle and begin walking (or skipping) as a group, all going in the same direction for 8 counts. After 8 counts, stomp your feet 3 times, clap your hands 3 times, stomp feet again 3 times, and clap hands again 3 times.
*This chorus section of music and movement will repeat after each verse.
Verse 1: Lift the right foot up when the high note plays and place the foot on the ground when the second, lower note plays. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 2: Lift the right foot up when the first note plays and place the foot on the ground with the lower note. Then lift the left foot up as the high note repeats, and place the left foot on the ground with the lower note. (Repeat chorus section)
Verse 3: Repeat the right foot and left foot, then lift the right knee up and gently kneel, placing the right knee on the floor. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 4: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee and then lift left knee and place on floor so that you are now kneeling on both knees. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle again for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 5: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, and then lift the right elbow toward the sky and gently place it on the ground. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 6: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right elbow, and then lift left elbow and place on the floor. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 7: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right elbow, left elbow, and then gently place the head on the floor. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

For this warm-up, explain to students that they will be learning different movements and styles of dance from around the world. It is recommended to choose music that supports each warm-up genre or use the playlist provided. Before each section of the warm-up, tell students what the style of dance is called and where it originates from.

Ballet (France)

Pliés — begin by standing tall in first position, feet in a turned out V, hands on your hips. Keeping the spine long, bend the knees as deeply as possible without the heels lifting off the ground. Repeat 6-8 times. *Can add arms in first position if student level allows. Continue the same exercise with feet wide in second position. When bending the knees, remind students to stay lifted in the spine and not to bend forward or stick hips back.

Tendues ­— begin in first position, hands on hips. Slide one foot forward until fully extended in a pointed position, keeping knees straight. Slide foot back to starting position. Repeat 6-8 times on one leg and then switch sides. Continue with tendues to the side and back on each leg.

Latin Dance

Hip/Torso Isolations — begin by standing tall, feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hands on your hips. Shift the hips from right to left, trying to keep the rest of the body still and controlled. Repeat right to left for 8 counts. Transition to shifting hips forward and back for 8 counts, with the rest of the body remaining still. Then move into combining all 4 directions (front, side, back, side) in both directions. After completing the hip isolations, repeat the entire sequence with the torso.

African Dance

Shoulder Isolations­ — stay in the standing posture (feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hands on your hips) and isolate the shoulders by lifting them up toward the ears, center/neutral, and then down toward the floor. The sequence will be “up, center, down, center.” Then remove the “center” position and alternate between shoulders going “up, down, up, down.” This can eventually be sped up to double speed. Repeat both sequences 6-8 times. Variations of this sequence can include alternating one shoulder at a time, rolling shoulders forward and back, etc.

Head/Neck Isolations — Following a similar pattern to the shoulder isolations, begin by rotating the neck side to side in the pattern, “right, center, left, center.” After repeating 4 times on each side, remove the pause in the center position, and simply look from side to side, on the beat. Repeat side to side 8 times. Continue this sequence with the head tilting side to side, keeping shoulders down, reaching right ear to right shoulder, center, and then left ear to left shoulder, and back to center. Repeat 4 times on each side, take out the center position and tilt right to left 8 times. Lastly, repeat the whole sequence isolating the head forward and back. Finish by rolling the neck in a slow circle, 2-4 times each direction, careful to keep the neck long and lengthened, so as not to stretch the neck too far in any single position.

Contemporary Dance (United States)

Fluid Stretch Flow - begin in second position, toes and knees gently turned out. Arms open wide to second position, and bend knees into deep grand plié, reminding students (just like in the ballet plié) to keep the spine lifted and keep hips under shoulders, as if you were squatting with your back against a wall. Repeat for 4 pliés. Keeping legs in second position, knees straight, move into a side stretch with the torso leaning to the right, left arm reaching up and overhead. Continue to a flat back stretch, swooping the right arm down by your side, while the left arm stays stretched overhead. Rotate the torso so the chest is facing the floor, trying to create a “tabletop” with your back, parallel to the floor, knees stay soft but not bent. Continue the stretch by folding forward over your right leg, nose toward the knee. Keeping the body folded forward, move the torso towards the middle, centered between both legs, before rolling up and repeating on the other side. Each of the 4 positions in this stretch can be introduced for a hold of 8 counts in each position, and then shortened to 4 counts each. Repeat the sequence on both sides 2-4 times.

Hip-Hop (United States)

Up/Down Bounce — Begin standing with feet hip distance apart, knees soft and bent, for the down bounce. Listening to the beat of the music, bend the knees to the beat and let your whole body “bounce” with the emphasis being down towards the ground. Keep the upper body loose and free, letting it add to the down bounce of the legs. Continue for 4 8-counts of music. *Option to add a small step, alternating feet, as the bounce continues. Transition to an up bounce where the knees will lengthen to a straight position (without locking or hyperextending the knees) and the rest of the body will lift, emphasizing the bounce on the “up” motion. Continue with the up bounce for 4 8-counts.

Freestyle — From the bounces, invite students to see where their bounce may lead. Let them groove to the music, explaining to them that in hip-hop, this is called “freestyle,” where you are free to show off your own unique style and dance in any way that makes you feel confident and happy. Remind students to respect other bodies while moving their own.

","

Folklórico Dance

Begin by telling students, “It’s time to travel in our imaginations to a different country in the world, one that is very close to us in the United States. Let’s go to Mexico and learn about Folklórico Dance! Folklórico dance is found all over Mexico, with different songs and dances in different regions, or areas of the country. The dances often include brightly colored costumes with upbeat and energetic movement. Whenever there are community gatherings or parties, dance is often part of the celebration.

“Think about your own dance experience. Does it also sometimes include costumes? Does dancing happen at your parties and celebrations?” Give a silent shake if you agree.

There are professional dancers who are trained in these dances but it is also a dance style where the whole community can join in. Let’s watch some children dancing Folklórico!”

“Remember when we watched the children doing African dance before, we looked for shapes, colors and feelings?” As students are watching, ask them to think about the following three questions:

  1. What types of shapes do you see them making with their bodies?
  2. What types of colors do you see represented in the dance?
  3. What feelings are they expressing?

Show students a video example of kids performing Folklórico dance. (Below you will find a list of suggested clips).

Suggested video clips (select one):

Un Poco Loco

Los Machetes

El Gavilancillo

Complete Dance #3 Choreography

Begin by placing students in window formation. Review the choreography from the previous classes and practice and repeat movements as necessary. Remember to switch lines periodically to ensure all students can see the teacher from the front row. Continue to teach the remaining 8-counts of choreography and review the full dance.

*The dance should be completed by this lesson. Choreography and song choice is at the discretion of the teacher. The choreography for this dance should be animal-themed and include elements of the steps and body positions students have learned in the preceding classes.

",,"

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

Ask students, “What were some of the similarities and differences between the dance in Africa vs. the dance in Mexico?” Invite 4-6 students to respond as a group.

Bows

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer Position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

To finish, ask students to gather their shoes and bring them back to the seated circle on the floor, the same way you began class. Instruct them to put their shoes back on, sit quietly, and place one hand on top of their head. When you see that they are ready, place a sticker on the hand that is resting on their head.

Review “Dancer” and “Audience Position.”

Dancer Position

“When I call out “Dancer Position!” that is your cue to stand up tall, feet together, knees pulled up straight, arms down by your sides (out of pockets or shirt sleeves). Head is lifted, shoulders down, eyes open, mouth closed. Body and eyes should be facing the teacher.” Model first, then have students practice this position all together and correct any student’s positions as needed.

Then tell them that you are going to practice this a few times to make sure they have it. When you say, “Be silly,” the students can move their bodies and talk in a silly way. Model this so students keep hands and bodies from touching or bothering anybody else. When they hear you say, “Dancer Position!” they should immediately stop their movement and freeze in the correct position. Tell students you will be using this phrase, “Dancer Position!” at the start and during each activity so that they are ready to listen and learn.

Audience Position

Have students return to a seated position in a circle. “There will also be times in dance class where you will be seated as an audience, watching other students dance. When I call out ‘Audience Position!,’ what do you think that might look like?” Identify students who are modeling elements of the correct position. Have students sit cross-legged, spine lifted tall, and hands on top of their knees. Their eyes should be open, mouth closed, and they should be looking at the person speaking or the dancer(s) performing. “When you hear me say, ‘Audience Position!,’ you should immediately stop your movement and speaking, and get into that seated position.”

<>
Check for Understanding: Practice these skills 3-5 times until all students respond consistently with accuracy.

column4: Favorite Move

Arrange students standing in a circle. Invite them to quickly take turns sharing their first name and showing their favorite dance move from the previous class. After each student shares, have the rest of the class respond by saying the student’s name and repeating the movement.

Hello/Goodbye Toes

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello toes!” followed by pointing the feet and saying, “Goodbye toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Finish by bending the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet. Lift the head up, trying to lengthen the spine and flex the feet saying, “Hello toes!” and then round the spine forward, nodding the head down and pointing the feet (keeping hands resting on the top of the foot/ankle) and say, “Goodbye toes.” Repeat 3-5 times.

Butterfly Trip

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be a real or pretend location). Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and “put on their brakes,” making a soft squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Make a Pizza

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to make a pretend pizza! Begin by asking, “What is the first thing we need to make a pizza?” Take 2-3 suggestions from students. Then say, “We need pizza dough!” Model and tell students to follow: shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (sauce, cheese, etc.). You can ask students for individual toppings and place them all around the imaginary pizza, getting a forward stretch each time. Remind students to try and keep their legs straight, “so their pizza stays flat and doesn’t get squished.”

Now it is time for the pizza to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pizza inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pizza to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pizza knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pizza is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pizza out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch), eat the other side, and then eat all the pizza in the middle, keeping legs as straight as possible.

Countdown

Bring all students to a standing position in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1.

Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Across the Floor Procedure

Before teaching across the floor exercises, begin by teaching how to prepare for across the floor work. First, explain that during dance classes, there is a designated area where they are allowed to dance (this will vary by site and classroom space).

Set up 3 identical courses, side by side, marking the starting point and end point for each course using the cones or poly dots. (This allows for 3 students to go across the floor at a time). Then mark the mid-way point in each course with a poly dot.

Have students create one long line, and ask the first 3 students to stand behind the starting cones or dots for each course. Explain that once the dancers reach the dot in the middle of the course, the next 3 students can line up and begin their turn. When the students reach the other end of the course, they will get in place at the back of the main line. Model the pattern of traffic to begin and end the course. Then model each exercise. Depending on the number of students and class time available, students can move across the floor 1-3 times per exercise.

Tiptoe Walks: Standing on tiptoe, hands on hips, students will walk across the floor, trying to stay high on their toes, not allowing the heels to touch the ground. Spine should be tall, knees should be pulled up straight and eyes looking forward, not down at the ground.

High-Knee Walks: Keeping feet flat, step forward and place one leg in parallel passé (bent knee, leg in parallel position with knee facing forward, toes attached to the inside of the standing leg). Teach students this position by getting out your “jar of glue” and brushing some glue onto the inside of the knee where your opposite foot can now “stick.”

Each time students come into passé, they should glue the inside of their pointed foot to the inside of the opposite knee. Keep hands on hips, walking across the floor, lifting alternating feet into passé for each step.

Focus on tall posture, eyes looking forward (not down at floor), and keeping upper-body controlled and still as the lower half moves. Students can advance to walking on tiptoe as well, once balance and body control have been established.

Two-Feet Jump: Glue the inside of the legs together, stand tall, hands on hips, eyes looking forward. Jump up and forward with both legs, keeping legs squeezing tightly together and feet pointed in the air.

Continue to jump across the floor, taking off and landing with both feet together until you reach the cone at the opposite side. Try to keep the upper body lifted through the chest, remaining as still and controlled as possible, with quiet feet.

One-Foot Hop: Stand tall, hands on hips, eyes looking forward. Hop on one foot from one side of the room to the other, trying to stay in a straight line, not falling over or losing control of the body. Switch feet half-way across the floor when they reach the poly dot at the mid-way point. Remind students to keep their upper body lifted through the chest, remaining as still and controlled as possible, with quiet feet.

Leap over the River: Place 3 large blue scarves on the floor at the midway point of each course. Explain to the students that the scarf represents a river, and they are going to jump over the “river.” Begin with the scarf gathered in a narrow line, and then increase the width of the river to encourage them to jump further each time. Instruct them to avoid stepping in the river (touching the scarf), and try to help them leap with one foot extending out in front and landing on the same front foot (like a grande jeté).

Collect and return all course materials (dots, cones, and scarves).

“Let’s warm up our bodies so that we can be fully prepared for our performance.”

Hello/Goodbye Toes

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello, toes!” followed by pointing the feet and saying, “Goodbye, toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Finish by bending the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet. Lift the head up, trying to lengthen the spine and flex the feet saying, “Hello, toes!” and then round the spine forward, nodding the head down and pointing the feet (keeping hands resting on the top of the foot/ankle) and say, “Goodbye, toes.” Repeat 3-5 times.

Butterfly Trip

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be a real or pretend location). Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and “put on their brakes,” making a soft squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Make a Pizza

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to make a pretend pizza! Begin by asking, “What is the first thing we need to make a pizza?” Take 2-3 suggestions from students.

Then say, “We need pizza dough!” Model and tell students to follow: shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (sauce, cheese, etc.). You can ask students for individual toppings and place them all around the imaginary pizza, getting a forward stretch each time. Remind students to try and keep their legs straight, “ so their pizza stays flat and doesn’t get squished.”

Now it is time for the pizza to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pizza inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pizza to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pizza knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pizza is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pizza out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch, eat the other side, and then eat all the pizza in the middle), keeping legs as straight as possible.

Countdown

Bring all students to a standing position in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1.

Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Roller Coaster Breathing

Hold one hand open out in front of you, fingers stretched wide, use the other hand as a pointer finger and place your finger below the thumb knuckle on the opposite hand. As you trace your finger up the outside of your thumb, take a deep breath in and imagine you are on a rollercoaster, slowly making your way to the top. Then, trace your thumb down the other side, breathing out in a silent “scream” as you go down the rollercoaster. Repeat on each finger for 5 full breaths.

Performance Option #1 (in the classroom):

f performing in the classroom for an audience,* designate the “stage” area and “audience” area. Line up students outside the class so they can enter and find their starting positions for the first dance they will perform.

*If there is not an outside audience, consider filming the performance and sharing the video link with families. Or, have half of the class be the audience while the other half performs! The importance of the performance is for students to experience the process and feel successful, no matter what form the “audience” takes.

Performance Option #2 (outside of the classroom)

If performing in a location outside the classroom (such as part of an assembly or other school event), use this final time to rehearse and review performance logistics.

  • Rehearse all of the dances for performance (including entrances, exits, and formations) in the area where students will be performing.
  • Answer any and all questions pertaining to how the performance will go, and what to expect.
    • Time, date, location, what to wear, what to bring (if anything)
    • Order of the dances and any other related events

If there is time after the performance for reflection, ask the students, “How did you feel right before the performance? How did you feel right after?” Invite students to respond. Encourage the rest of the students to “silent shake” in agreement if they liked similar things being shared.

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer Position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

Circle-Up

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. OK, show me your thumb scale!” Briefly acknowledge each student’s level with a neutral, appreciative response.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students, “Today we are going to perform the ‘Giraffes Can’t Dance’ story for each other, using dance to bring it to life!”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What are some of the dances that the different animals perform in ‘Giraffes Can’t Dance?’” If you have the book, show students the pages where the animals dance in different styles.

Write these on the board and demonstrate simple examples of the following dances and steps:

  1. Skip
  2. Prance
  3. Waltz
  4. Rock ‘n’ Roll
  5. Tango
  6. Cha-Cha
  7. Scottish Reel
",,"
Dance Telephone

Arrange students evenly into 3 lines, front to back, standing in Dancer Position, and using the whole floor space so everyone has room to move. All students should be facing the same direction (toward the designated “back” of the room). Ask the first student in each of the 3 lines to turn and face the front (while everyone else remains facing the back).

In this variation, the teacher will demonstrate a different movement for each line. Show each line leader the move for their line, and ask them to repeat the movement back to you to ensure they accurately copied the movement. Then, have each of the three students turn around to face their line, tap the next student in line on the shoulder, cueing them to turn toward the front, and demonstrate the exact same movement as closely as possible to what they saw originally. The student second in line will then tap the next student in line on the shoulder and repeat the movement as closely as possible.

Play continues down the line, similar to the game of telephone. When it gets to the end of the line, ask the final three students to make their way to the front of the room, and ask all students to turn to face the front. Have each of the final three students demonstrate the movement they learned, and then compare it to the teacher’s original movement.
Ask students, “Did the movement change or did it remain close to the original?” Invite 3-5 students to respond.

For this warm-up, the movements will loosely follow the story of “The Very Hungry Caterpillar” by Eric Carle, exploring the progression from caterpillar, to chrysalis, to butterfly. In each exercise, demonstrate the new movement first, then have students follow.

Caterpillar Stretch (Cat/Cow)

Instruct students to think about how a caterpillar moves, inching, bending, and scooting to travel. Begin on hands and knees; demonstrate for students how to slowly bend the spine -- moving from an arched, rounded back to a concave arch in the reverse direction. The movement should feel continuous and rolling, like a caterpillar.

Growing Caterpillar (Down Dog/Cobra + Child’s Pose)

From hands and knees, push up to a downward facing dog position, arms and legs extended in an upside “V” shape. Move like a caterpillar smoothly from down dog into cobra, extending the chest up and open, then roll back into down dog. Roll through the two positions 3-5 times and then finish in child’s pose, pretending you are a caterpillar hiding from the birds above. Kneel on the ground, allowing your spine to round over your legs and fold forward.

Heel/Toe/Leg Stretch

Come to a seated position, grab heels or toes, walk legs out like a caterpillar inching forward (pretending to be a caterpillar finding food), then walk legs in (to hide from the birds). Repeat 4-6 times.

Food Splits

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Bend over each leg and eat imaginary food off the tops of each leg and all the food in the middle space created by the seated second split position. Ask students for suggestions for what type of food the caterpillar should eat.

Tree Pose

“Now let’s stand up and get into ‘Dancer Position’. Let’s pretend to find a tree in which to make your cocoon (tree pose). Raise your hand if you can tell us what a ‘cocoon’ is?” Invite 1-2 students to respond.

Begin by standing tall in mountain pose and lift one foot off the ground balancing on the standing leg. Bend the knee of the lifted leg and place the foot on the inside of the standing leg, either low at the ankle, or just above the knee. (The higher the foot is placed along the leg, the more challenging to balance; just ensure that students are not placing their foot directly on the knee joint).

Place the arms out to the side to help balance and then lift arms up into “branches” of the tree. Hold the balance, then switch legs.

Cocoon

“Audience Position. Now let’s make our bodies into a cocoon.” Lay on your back in a tight ball, roll back and forth, massaging the spine. As an added challenge, start seated in the tight ball, balancing with the feet slightly off the ground. Roll back and then return to a seated position, trying not to let your feet touch the ground at any time. Demonstrate, then students copy.

Butterfly

“Now our cocoon will turn into a butterfly!” Remain in a seated position and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you have now become butterflies and get to fly to your first flower to find nectar. “Land” on the flower by gently pushing down on the tops of the knees for a stretch, bend forward and “drink” the nectar while getting a deeper stretch through the legs and spine.

","

Giraffes Can’t Dance (Improvised Story)

Explain to students that they will now perform an improvised dance for the rest of the class to the story of “Giraffes Can’t Dance.” “Remember last time when we chose characters and elements of the story and used dance to show the beginning, middle and end? Today we will do a performance of the story again, in front of a class audience.” Begin by dividing the students into 3 groups and invite the first group onto the “stage” while the rest of the class sits in Audience Position. (The three groups can be different from the previous class).

Encourage students to add emotions and expression to the characters they choose to act out, making the performance more interesting to watch for the audience. “Try to remember some of the dances the other animals did so you can do them yourselves, like waltzing or skipping or prancing.” Refer to the list of dances from earlier. Read the beginning of the story aloud (from the physical book) and have the first group move/act out each part of the story for the audience. Encourage students to use the text from the story combined with their imaginations to tell the story through their bodies and movement. Keep the structure of this activity loose: students can act out any character or element they choose! For example, there can be multiple dancers who choose to be the giraffe, or even dancers who choose to be an object such as the tree or moon.

Switch to group two for the middle section of the story and then finish with group three. <>

Dance #3 Choreography (Continued)

Arrange students in window formation. Review the first section of choreography with students, practice and repeat movements as necessary. Remember to switch lines periodically to ensure all students can see the teacher from the front row. Continue to teach the next two to four 8-counts of choreography and add on to the previous steps.

*While choreography and song choice is at the discretion of the teacher, the movement should be reflective of the steps and dance elements students have learned in recent classes.

",,"

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

Ask students, “What feelings and emotions were expressed in “Giraffes Can’t Dance,” either by Gerald, or the other animals, or the cricket? How do you know?” Invite 4-6 students to respond as a group.

Bows

Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Remind students of the three bow choices they can choose from by demonstrating each one:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer Position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer Position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

To finish, ask students to gather their shoes and bring them back to the seated circle on the floor, the same way you began class. Instruct them to put their shoes back on, sit quietly, and place one hand on top of their head. When you see that they are ready, place a sticker on the hand that is resting on their head.

Favorite Sport

“In the last two classes you shared one of your favorite sports and a movement that represents that sport. See if you can remember the sport and movement you chose. For example, if your sport was soccer, your movement might show a low kick, as if kicking a ball.” In this class, go around the circle and ask each student to share their sport using only the movement, and ask the rest of the class to guess the sport.

Follow the Leader

Remind students that they get to lead the warm-up!

Review the procedure:

  1. Arrange students in window formation. Teacher stands at the front of the group.
  2. The teacher demonstrates a simple stretch or warm-up movement that students follow.
  3. The teacher will then walk behind a student and tap them gently on the shoulder.
  4. Once tapped, the student will move to the front of the room, and the teacher will stand in the student’s position in window formation.
  5. The student in front will lead the group in a new stretch or warm-up movement. Students follow.
  6. The teacher will then tap the shoulder of another student who will go to the front of the room, high-five the current student leader to switch spots, and lead the class in another new movement.
  7. The student in front returns to their original spot in the window formation.
  8. The teacher continues to tap on students to take turns leading the warm-up.

Review the Warm-Up Guidelines

Explain to students that there are a few ways to make their turn as leader successful. “The purpose of a warm-up is to safely prepare our body and mind for dance. This means that any move you do must be safe and possible for all dancers in the room (ie. don’t go into the splits, just because you can – that is not a move that everyone can do safely or at all!).” Next, remind them that in order to warm up the body evenly, any stretch or move that you do on one side of the body, you must also do on the other side. Lastly, “If you can’t think of a move to do, roll your wrists in a circle while you think of a move.”

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students, “Today we are going to explore shapes in dance: shapes in our bodies and movement, as well as shapes you can make traveling through the space.”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What are some examples of shapes you already know? Do you see any in the room?” Invite 3-5 students to respond.

Remind the other students that they can use the “silent shake/applause” hand signal if a student shares the same shape they were thinking of.

",,"
Body Shapes

Ask students to stand in the circle in Dancer Position. “Do you think you could make a shape with your body? You can use one part of your body (such as your arms), or try and use the whole thing!” Rotate around the circle, allowing each student to create a shape and have the rest of the class guess the shapes.

Encourage students to explore new ways to represent a shape that has already been shared. For example, if a student makes a “V” shape with their arms overhead, another student could make a “V” with their legs or feet.

Shape Breathing

Seated in a circle, “Audience Position!,” legs crossed, spine tall, explain that you are going to breathe, using shapes as your guide.

  • Square: Instruct students to trace a square shape In the air with their finger, beginning at the top of the square. Inhale for 4 counts as you trace your finger along the top line of the imaginary square, then hold your breath for 4 counts as you trace the line down the side, then exhale for 4 counts as you draw the bottom line, and hold your breath for 4 counts as you draw the final line up to close the shape. Demonstrate, then have students copy. Repeat 3-5 times.
  • Triangle: Begin at the bottom of the imaginary triangle shape and trace in the air the first side of the triangle, moving the finger up at an angle while inhaling for 3 counts. As you trace the second side of the triangle, hold the breath for 3 counts, complete the last side of the triangle by exhaling for 3 counts. Demonstrate, then have students copy. Repeat 3-5 times.
  • Lazy 8 / Infinity: Imagine the number 8, lying on its side (like the infinity symbol). Model the shape. Begin in the center of the 8 and trace the finger around one loop as you inhale for 4 counts, then continue moving the finger around the shape, exhaling for 4 counts as you trace the other loop. Repeat 3-5 times.
  • Circle: Use your finger to trace a circle shape in the air, beginning at the bottom, and moving up. Inhale as you trace the circle up and around, exhale as you continue to trace the circle down and around. Demonstrate, then students copy. The circle can start small with shorter breaths and then grow to make larger circles with longer breaths.

Remain seated and have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the sides of their legs. Begin by flexing the feet and notice what kind of line the feet make (straight line), “like a tall building!” Then, point the feet towards the floor and notice the curved line, “like a bridge,” made by the pointed feet. Demonstrate and then have students repeat 4-6 times.
