Remain seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. “The position of our legs formed a diamond shape!” Instruct students to lift their spine into a tall, straight line, gently pressing down on the tops of the knees to get a stretch. With legs open wide in seated second position, paint shapes on the floor between their legs. Encourage them to paint large shapes, stretching their arms and bodies forward to get a stretch in each position. Suggested shapes: circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, heart.

Seven Jumps:

Begin by standing in a circle in Dancer Position. Share with students that the next activity is from a popular folk song and dance originating in Denmark, a country in Europe, called, “The Seven Jumps.” It is danced to the folk song of the same name performed by Shenanigans.
Intro

The song begins with a series of three sustained chords, students will listen to these chords as they prepare for the first movement section. Play the first notes of the song, and ask students to “Nod your head if you hear these three chords.”
Chorus

Gently hold hands in the circle and begin walking (or skipping) as a group, all going in the same direction for 8 counts. After 8 counts, stomp your feet 3 times, clap your hands 3 times, stomp feet again 3 times, and clap hands again 3 times.
*This chorus section of music and movement will repeat after each verse.
Verse 1: Lift the right foot up when the high note plays and place the foot on the ground when the second, lower note plays. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 2: Lift the right foot up when the first note plays and place the foot on the ground with the lower note. Then lift the left foot up as the high note repeats, and place the left foot on the ground with the lower note. (Repeat chorus section)
Verse 3: Repeat the right foot and left foot, then lift the right knee up and gently kneel, placing the right knee on the floor. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 4: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee and then lift left knee and place on floor so that you are now kneeling on both knees. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle again for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 5: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, and then lift the right elbow toward the sky and gently place it on the ground. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 6: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right elbow, and then lift left elbow and place on the floor. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

Verse 7: Repeat right foot, left foot, right knee, left knee, right elbow, left elbow, and then gently place the head on the floor. Then, quickly get up to begin walking around the circle for the chorus. (Repeat chorus section)

For this warm-up, explain to students that they will be learning different movements and styles of dance from around the world. It is recommended to choose music that supports each warm-up genre or use the playlist provided. Before each section of the warm-up, tell students what the style of dance is called and where it originates from.

Ballet (France)

Pliés — begin by standing tall in first position, feet in a turned out V, hands on your hips. Keeping the spine long, bend the knees as deeply as possible without the heels lifting off the ground. Repeat 6-8 times. *Can add arms in first position if student level allows. Continue the same exercise with feet wide in second position. When bending the knees, remind students to stay lifted in the spine and not to bend forward or stick hips back.

Tendues ­— begin in first position, hands on hips. Slide one foot forward until fully extended in a pointed position, keeping knees straight. Slide foot back to starting position. Repeat 6-8 times on one leg and then switch sides. Continue with tendues to the side and back on each leg.

Latin Dance

Hip/Torso Isolations — begin by standing tall, feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hands on your hips. Shift the hips from right to left, trying to keep the rest of the body still and controlled. Repeat right to left for 8 counts. Transition to shifting hips forward and back for 8 counts, with the rest of the body remaining still. Then move into combining all 4 directions (front, side, back, side) in both directions. After completing the hip isolations, repeat the entire sequence with the torso.

African Dance

Shoulder Isolations­ — stay in the standing posture (feet hip-width apart, knees slightly bent, hands on your hips) and isolate the shoulders by lifting them up toward the ears, center/neutral, and then down toward the floor. The sequence will be “up, center, down, center.” Then remove the “center” position and alternate between shoulders going “up, down, up, down.” This can eventually be sped up to double speed. Repeat both sequences 6-8 times. Variations of this sequence can include alternating one shoulder at a time, rolling shoulders forward and back, etc.

Head/Neck Isolations — Following a similar pattern to the shoulder isolations, begin by rotating the neck side to side in the pattern, “right, center, left, center.” After repeating 4 times on each side, remove the pause in the center position, and simply look from side to side, on the beat. Repeat side to side 8 times. Continue this sequence with the head tilting side to side, keeping shoulders down, reaching right ear to right shoulder, center, and then left ear to left shoulder, and back to center. Repeat 4 times on each side, take out the center position and tilt right to left 8 times. Lastly, repeat the whole sequence isolating the head forward and back. Finish by rolling the neck in a slow circle, 2-4 times each direction, careful to keep the neck long and lengthened, so as not to stretch the neck too far in any single position.

Contemporary Dance (United States)

Fluid Stretch Flow - begin in second position, toes and knees gently turned out. Arms open wide to second position, and bend knees into deep grand plié, reminding students (just like in the ballet plié) to keep the spine lifted and keep hips under shoulders, as if you were squatting with your back against a wall. Repeat for 4 pliés. Keeping legs in second position, knees straight, move into a side stretch with the torso leaning to the right, left arm reaching up and overhead. Continue to a flat back stretch, swooping the right arm down by your side, while the left arm stays stretched overhead. Rotate the torso so the chest is facing the floor, trying to create a “tabletop” with your back, parallel to the floor, knees stay soft but not bent. Continue the stretch by folding forward over your right leg, nose toward the knee. Keeping the body folded forward, move the torso towards the middle, centered between both legs, before rolling up and repeating on the other side. Each of the 4 positions in this stretch can be introduced for a hold of 8 counts in each position, and then shortened to 4 counts each. Repeat the sequence on both sides 2-4 times.

Hip-Hop (United States)

Up/Down Bounce — Begin standing with feet hip distance apart, knees soft and bent, for the down bounce. Listening to the beat of the music, bend the knees to the beat and let your whole body “bounce” with the emphasis being down towards the ground. Keep the upper body loose and free, letting it add to the down bounce of the legs. Continue for 4 8-counts of music. *Option to add a small step, alternating feet, as the bounce continues. Transition to an up bounce where the knees will lengthen to a straight position (without locking or hyperextending the knees) and the rest of the body will lift, emphasizing the bounce on the “up” motion. Continue with the up bounce for 4 8-counts.

Freestyle — From the bounces, invite students to see where their bounce may lead. Let them groove to the music, explaining to them that in hip-hop, this is called “freestyle,” where you are free to show off your own unique style and dance in any way that makes you feel confident and happy. Remind students to respect other bodies while moving their own.

Social/Emotional: Students will learn about other people, cultures and lifestyles, while developing empathy and cross-cultural understanding.
Check-In: Students show a sense of trust and belonging, and experience acceptance and inclusion.

Warm-Up: Students demonstrate skills of listening and following directions, and experience dance moves from other cultures. Students move their body with control and body awareness as they rehearse their choreographed dance. Students are asked to reflect on the culture of Africa as embodied by dance.

Circle-Up

Arrange students in a circle on the floor, seated in a cross-legged position, hands on top of knees.

Thumb-Scale Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Any level is the right level, as long as you are being truthful. I really want to know how you are doing today. If you are having a great day, give me a thumbs up. If you are not having a good day, give me a thumbs down. And if it is somewhere in the middle, that is great too! OK, show me your thumb scale!” Briefly acknowledge each student’s level with a neutral, appreciative response.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today’s lesson is going to explore various ways we can move our bodies as dancers.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Can someone raise a quiet hand and tell me, what is dance?” Allow 2-3 students to respond.

Then ask all students, “Has anyone ever taken a dance class before?” Ask 2-3 students to share. After each response, ask if anyone else in the group has had a similar experience. For example, if a student responds, “Yes, I take ballet classes.” Ask the whole class, “Does anyone else take ballet classes? Raise a silent hand if you also have taken ballet.”

column1: Check for Understanding: “Dance is when we move our bodies, usually to music. We might dance to show an idea, or a feeling or an action. Show me with a thumbs up if you like to dance?”

Dancer Position

Explain to students that you have a few special rules for dance class that might be a little different from the normal rules in the classroom. Given that there will be many times when they are moving throughout the room and having fun, you need to set some rules to make sure everyone stays safe and listens well – leaving as much time to dance together as possible.

“When I call out “Dancer Position!” that is your cue to stand up tall, feet together, knees pulled up straight, arms down by your sides (out of pockets or shirt sleeves). Head is lifted, shoulders down, eyes open, mouth closed. Body and eyes should be facing the teacher.” Model first, then have students practice this position all together and correct any student’s positions as needed.

Then tell them that you are going to practice this a few times to make sure they have it. When you say, “Be silly,” the students can move their bodies and talk in a silly way. Model this so students keep hands and bodies from touching or bothering anybody else. When they hear you say, “Dancer Position!” they should immediately stop their movement and freeze in the correct position. Tell students you will be using this phrase, “Dancer Position!” at the start and during each activity so that they are ready to listen and learn.

Audience Position

Have students return to a seated position in a circle. “There will also be times in dance class where you will be seated as an audience, watching other students dance. When I call out ‘Audience Position!’ what do you think that might look like?” Identify students who are modeling elements of the correct position. Have students sit cross-legged, spine lifted tall, and hands on top of their knees. Their eyes should be open, mouth closed, and they should be looking at the person speaking or the dancer(s) performing. “When you hear me say, ‘Audience Position!’ you should immediately stop your movement and speaking, and get into that seated position.”

<>
Check for Understanding: Practice these skills 3-5 times until all students respond consistently with accuracy.

column4: Favorite Move
Begin by asking students to stand in a circle. Invite students to quickly take turns sharing their first name and showing one of their favorite dance moves.
After each student shares, have the rest of the class respond by saying the student’s name and repeating the movement.

Hello/Goodbye Toes

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and safely dance together. Audience position!” Begin seated in a circle and model each warm-up exercise for the students first.

Have students bring their legs straight out in front of them, spine lifted tall, hands by the side of the legs. Begin by flexing the feet and saying, “Hello toes!” followed by pointing the feet and saying, “Goodbye toes.” Continue to point and flex, greeting the feet in each position. Students can also alternate one foot at a time and play with tempo – going fast and slow to provide variety.

Finish by bending the knees in toward the chest, grab onto the toes, and slowly walk the feet out away from the chest, working towards straightening the legs while still holding onto the feet. Lift the head up, trying to lengthen the spine and flex the feet saying, “Hello toes!” and then round the spine forward, nodding the head down and pointing the feet (keeping hands resting on the top of the foot/ankle) and say, “Goodbye toes.” Repeat 3-5 times.

Butterfly Trip

Begin seated and have students bend both knees, bringing the soles of the feet together and opening knees out to the sides. Hands can rest on the tops of the ankles. Explain that you are now butterflies and get to fly to your favorite places. Then ask students one at a time* where they would like to fly today (can be a real or pretend location). Then instruct all students to “flap their wings” and fly to their destination. Gently push down on the tops of the knees to increase the stretch and “put on their brakes,” making a soft squeaky brake sound.

*If you have a large group (more than 15 students), ask to hear from just 5 students to save time.

Make a Pizza

Open the legs wide into a seated, second position split, or V-shape. Tell the students that you are now going to make a pretend pizza! Begin by asking, “What is the first thing we need to make a pizza?” Take 2-3 suggestions from students. Then say, “We need pizza dough!” Model and tell students to follow: shape the imaginary dough in your hands, plop it onto the ground between your legs and begin spreading the dough along the inside of each leg, toward the toes, and all along the center space (getting a forward fold stretch in all directions). Then ask students what comes next (sauce, cheese, etc.). You can ask students for individual toppings and place them all around the imaginary pizza, getting a forward stretch each time. Remind students to try and keep their legs straight, “so their pizza stays flat and doesn’t get squished.”

Now it is time for the pizza to go in the oven. Open a big oven door, slide the pizza inside, close the door and set the timer. Have students wait for the pizza to cook by placing their chin on their elbows, resting on the floor in front of their legs, working to keep their pizza knees straight and open out to either side. Tilt the head side to side and make a tick-tock sound for the timer. After 10-15 seconds, shout, “Ding!” indicating the pizza is done cooking and ready to eat. Open the oven, pull the pizza out and blow on both sides/legs and in the middle to help it cool. Then eat one side (bending over one leg to get the stretch), eat the other side, and then eat all the pizza in the middle, keeping legs as straight as possible.

Countdown

Bring all students to a standing position in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Begin by lifting one arm overhead and shaking it while counting down from 8 to 1. Lower the arm, then lift the other arm and shake while counting down. Then shake one leg, and then the other, each time counting down from 8 to 1.

Finally, shake your whole body and count down from 8 to 1. All students should be counting out loud and moving their bodies. Repeat the sequence (arm, arm, leg, leg, body), counting down by one less number each time. 7 to 1, 6 to 1, 5 to 1, etc. Continue until you shake each body part 1 time and finish with one big final shake of the body to get any last wiggles out!

Free Dance with Scarves

Distribute a small colored scarf to each student and have them find a space in the room within the designated “safe space” for dancing. Instruct them to spread out with enough room to avoid bumping into any other dancers. For this activity, there are a few additional rules to ensure safety:

No Talking: this is about exploring dance with your body, not your voice. (A little laughter is inevitable and totally ok.)

No Touching: this means that you should not touch any other dancer or anything else in the room (such as desks, chairs, things on the wall, etc.)

No Dancing on the Floor: bodies need to stay standing for this exercise to ensure that no fingers or other body parts get stepped on, and no one accidentally trips over another dancer.

*If you have a large group, this activity can be done in 2 groups with the other group watching off to the side of the dance space.

“Dancer Position!” Play three contrasting songs and see how the movement changes between each piece of music. <>

Return to a seated position in a circle on the floor. “Audience Position.”

Ask students, “Who can tell us what feeling you acted out with your scarf while you danced today? Who can share which music they enjoyed dancing to most: the first song, the second song or the third song? Why?” Allow 6-8 students to respond.

Bows

For the first class, explain to students that you will end every class with a custom bow and a sticker celebrating their great effort, focus, and participation. Ask students to stand up in the circle, “Dancer Position!” Demonstrate, teach, and practice the three bows that they can choose from:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Dancer position.”

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Dancer position.”

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

To finish, ask students to gather their shoes and bring them back to the seated circle on the floor, the same way you began class. Instruct them to put their shoes back on, sit quietly, and place one hand on top of their head. When you see that they are ready, place a sticker on the hand that is resting on their head.
